name: Google Cast / Chromecast
category: Multi-mode wireless display/media handoff: primarily media-URL-casting (sender hands a media URL to a receiver app) plus screen/tab-mirroring (real-time A/V streaming). Also does app-launch (via app IDs, historically DIAL). Transport-substrate for both is a protobuf-over-TLS control channel.
summary: Google Cast is Google's protocol + SDK for a "sender" (phone/tablet/laptop/browser) to discover a "receiver" (a Cast-capable TV, dongle, or speaker) on the LAN, launch a receiver application, and either hand it a media URL to fetch and play itself, or stream real-time mirrored A/V to it. Chromecast is the hardware/brand that popularized it; "Chromecast built-in" (2016-2024) and now "Google Cast" (2024+) is the same receiver technology licensed into third-party TVs and speakers. Two protocol layers matter: a JSON/protobuf-over-TLS control channel (CASTv2, TCP:8009, discovered via mDNS) and, for mirroring, a separate WebRTC-style RTP/RTCP media path over UDP. A TLS-level device-authentication challenge/response backed by a Google-rooted certificate chain is the main blocker to building a fully interoperable open receiver.
transmitterPlatforms: Android: native Cast SDK / Cast Application Framework (CAF) sender library; also baked into many Google apps and Android system 'Cast' UI
iOS: native CAF sender SDK
Web/Chrome: Cast is built directly into Chrome (Presentation API + internal Cast implementation; the old separate 'Google Cast' extension is obsolete). Also Chromium-based Edge etc.
Chrome OS / Chromebooks: built-in tab + desktop casting
Third-party media apps embed the CAF sender SDK to add a Cast button

Open-source senders: pychromecast (Python, used by Home Assistant), node-castv2 / node-castv2-client (Node), catt (CLI), OpenCastSwift (Swift) — these speak CASTv2 and, notably, do NOT enforce receiver device-auth, so they interoperate with open receivers
receiverPlatforms: Chromecast dongles (gen1 2013, gen2 2015, Ultra 2016, gen3 2018) — media receiver only, no app UI
Chromecast Audio (audio-only sink)
Chromecast with Google TV (2020 4K, 2022 HD) — Android TV/Google TV device that is also a Cast receiver
Google TV Streamer (2024, $99) — the successor set-top box, Cast receiver built in
Android TV / Google TV smart TVs and boxes (Sony, TCL, Hisense, Nvidia Shield, etc.)
Third-party TVs/speakers/displays licensing 'Chromecast built-in' / 'Google Cast' (LG webOS, some Samsung, Vizio, Bose, Sonos, JBL, Nest Audio/Hub)
Coming to cars via Android Automotive (announced I/O 2024)
Unofficial/open: openscreen standalone_receiver (Google's own C++ ref impl), Shanocast (mirroring receiver hack), node-castv2 server (non-functional without auth)
howItWorks: Discovery: sender does an mDNS query for _googlecast._tcp.local; receivers answer with A records + TXT (friendly name, model, app availability). DIAL (SSDP-based, co-developed by Netflix/YouTube) is a legacy/parallel discovery+app-launch path used e.g. by YouTube. Control channel (CASTv2): sender opens a TLS connection to the receiver on TCP port 8009. Framing is a 4-byte big-endian length prefix followed by a protobuf 'CastMessage' (protocol version, source_id/destination_id like 'sender-0'/'receiver-0', a string 'namespace' selecting the logical channel, and a STRING (usually JSON) or BINARY payload). Namespaces multiplex sub-protocols: tp.connection (CONNECT/CLOSE virtual connections), tp.heartbeat (PING/PONG ~every 5s or the link drops), tp.deviceauth (the device-auth challenge/response, binary/protobuf), receiver (LAUNCH by app ID, STOP, GET_STATUS, SET_VOLUME → RECEIVER_STATUS), and media (LOAD/PLAY/PAUSE/SEEK → MEDIA_STATUS). Two content models: (1) Media-URL casting — sender sends a LOAD with a media URL (HLS/DASH/Smooth/MP4) and metadata; the receiver app fetches and plays the stream itself over its own internet connection; the sender is just a remote control. (2) Mirroring/remoting — a separate real-time path negotiated WebRTC-style: an Offer/Answer exchange (carried over the CASTv2 control channel) agrees codecs (VP8/H264 video, Opus/AAC audio), AES media-encryption keys (aes_key/aes_iv_mask), and a UDP port; media then flows over a custom Cast RTP/RTCP implementation over UDP. Receiver side: the launched receiver is a web app (CAF Web Receiver, an HTML/JS page loaded from a URL registered to the app ID) running in a Cast runtime, or a native Android TV Receiver.
lowerLevelProtocols: mDNS / DNS-SD (_googlecast._tcp.local) for discovery
DIAL (SSDP/UPnP-derived) for legacy discovery + app launch (YouTube, Netflix)
TLS over TCP port 8009 for the CASTv2 control channel
Protocol Buffers (CastMessage framing; deviceauth messages) with a 32-bit big-endian length prefix
JSON payloads inside CastMessage for most namespaces (receiver, media, connection, heartbeat)
Custom Cast RTP/RTCP over UDP for mirroring/streaming media
HLS, MPEG-DASH, Smooth Streaming, and progressive MP4 for URL-based media delivery
AES for mirroring media encryption; Widevine (CENC) for URL-based DRM content
authEncryption: Two distinct layers. (1) Transport: the CASTv2 channel is always TLS, but the receiver presents a self-signed cert, so senders must accept it — TLS alone does not authenticate the device. (2) Device Authentication (over urn:x-cast:com.google.cast.tp.deviceauth): the sender sends a challenge; the receiver returns a manifest containing a per-device certificate, the product-line Intermediate CA (ICA) cert, and a signature (SHA-256 hash of the receiver's TLS peer cert, signed with the device's private key; RSA-2048, X.509). The sender re-hashes the peer cert, verifies the signature with the device cert's public key, then verifies device-cert → ICA → Google Cast Root CA (root embedded in Chrome/Android). The device private key is fused into the SoC on genuine Chromecasts and not readable by on-device code — this is what makes forging a receiver hard. Crucially, enforcement is a SENDER-side choice: Chrome and official SDK senders verify the full chain (and reject an untrusted/expired chain — this caused the March 2025 gen-2 outage when the ICA expired), while open-source senders (pychromecast, node-castv2, catt) skip device-auth entirely and happily talk to any receiver. Mirroring media is separately AES-encrypted with keys from the Offer/Answer. URL DRM: protected streams use Widevine (and PlayReady on some smart-TV receivers); handling license URLs/auth requires a Custom Web Receiver.

openImplementations.name: Open Screen Library (chromium/openscreen)
openImplementations.maturity: Google-maintained reference implementation; production-adjacent (part of Chromium)
openImplementations.notes: Google's OWN open-source implementation of Cast discovery, application control, and streaming, including cast_sender, cast_receiver, and standalone_receiver. This is the single most important artifact for anyone building a receiver — it's the actual protocol logic in the open. But it ships no valid Google-signed device certificate, so a receiver built from it cannot pass device-auth against Chrome/official senders without a real (extracted or leaked) cert chain.

openImplementations.name: Shanocast
openImplementations.notes: A working mirroring receiver built on openscreen's standalone_receiver. Bypasses device-auth by replaying ~795 precomputed signatures and a private key/cert extracted from the 'AirReceiver' Android app, exploiting that Chrome's enforce_nonce_checking is false (accepts replayed signatures). Author expects it to break eventually. Demonstrates both that an open receiver is technically buildable AND that the cert chain is the wall.

openImplementations.name: node-castv2 / node-castv2-client
openImplementations.notes: Best low-level CASTv2 client reference. Explicitly warns its Server side is 'pretty useless because device authentication gets in the way for now (and maybe for good)' — a clean statement of the receiver blocker.

openImplementations.name: PyChromecast
openImplementations.notes: De-facto reference open sender. Does auto-discovery and full media/receiver control; does not verify receiver device-auth, so it interoperates with open receivers.

openImplementations.name: catt (Cast All The Things)
openImplementations.notes: CLI sender on top of PyChromecast; useful for testing receivers.

openImplementations.name: OpenCastSwift
openImplementations.notes: Swift Cast SDK reimplementation inspired by pychromecast/node-castv2-client.

closedImplementations.name: Cast Application Framework (CAF) — Web Receiver SDK
closedImplementations.notes: The official receiver runtime. A CAF Web Receiver is an HTML/JS app (loaded from a registered URL) that uses cast.framework; it handles adaptive streaming (HLS/DASH/Smooth) and MP4 out of the box via Shaka Player. Three tiers: Default Media Receiver (no customization), Styled Media Receiver (CSS branding), and Custom Web Receiver (full logic, needed for DRM auth, ads, custom license URLs). Free SDK but the receiver runtime and the Cast platform on-device are closed.
closedImplementations.licensing: SDK free; app must be registered in the Cast Developer Console to get an app ID (a fee historically applied). Publishing to real (non-dev) receivers requires Google approval.

closedImplementations.name: CAF Sender SDKs (Android, iOS, Web)
closedImplementations.notes: Official closed sender libraries; Web sender is built into Chrome. Handle discovery, connection, device-auth, session and media control so app devs don't touch the wire protocol.

closedImplementations.name: Chromecast built-in / Google Cast licensing program
closedImplementations.notes: To ship a device that is a genuine, Chrome-trusted Cast receiver, an OEM must join Google's Cast-for-partners program: Google provisions per-device certificates chaining to the Cast Root CA (the fused-key + ICA scheme). This certification/provisioning is the gate that open receivers cannot pass.
closedImplementations.licensing: Partner/certification program under NDA; certificate provisioning controlled by Google.

closedImplementations.name: Cast on-device platform (Eureka firmware)
closedImplementations.notes: The proprietary firmware on Chromecast dongles (a stripped Android/ChromeOS hybrid). Not open; device keys fused into SoC.

protocolDocs: Mixed. The SENDER/receiver-app developer surface is officially and publicly documented (developers.google.com/cast: CAF sender + Web Receiver APIs, media message formats). The WIRE protocol is only semi-public: the CastMessage protobuf lives in the open Chromium tree (extensions/common/api/cast_channel and openscreen/cast), and the entire discovery/control/streaming stack is implemented in the open in chromium/openscreen — so it is effectively 'open via source' rather than via a formal spec. The device-authentication scheme and certificate provisioning are NOT publicly specified and are understood mainly through reverse-engineering. Key reverse-eng writeups: thibauts/node-castv2 (framing/namespaces), dylanmckay/gcast PROTOCOL.md, Tristan Penman's device-authentication series (2025) and OakBits 'Receiver Authentication' (cert chain), yingtongli.me (disabling device auth via Xposed), and xakcop.com/shanocast (receiver via openscreen + auth bypass).
receiverFeasibility: Building an open receiver splits into two very different difficulties. The PROTOCOL mechanics are entirely achievable and largely already done: advertise _googlecast._tcp via mDNS, run a TLS server on 8009, parse the length-prefixed CastMessage protobuf, implement the connection/heartbeat/receiver/media namespaces, and for mirroring run the Offer/Answer + custom RTP/RTCP over UDP — Google's own openscreen library gives you all of this as C++ source. The BLOCKER is device authentication: genuine Chrome and official-SDK senders issue a deviceauth challenge and reject any receiver whose signature doesn't chain a fused-device-key signature up through a product ICA to the Google Cast Root CA. There is no legitimate way to obtain such a cert without joining Google's partner/certification program; every open 'receiver that works with Chrome' (e.g. Shanocast) does it by extracting a real device key/cert from a licensed product and replaying signatures, which is fragile and arguably a licensing/security violation. However — and this is the practical escape hatch — open SENDERS (pychromecast, node-castv2, catt) do NOT enforce device-auth, so an open receiver that simply ignores/answers deviceauth trivially can fully interoperate with the open-source sender ecosystem (and thus with Home Assistant, CLI tools, etc.), just not with Chrome or unmodified vendor apps. Secondary blockers: DRM (Widevine/PlayReady) content can't be decrypted without a provisioned CDM, and screen-mirroring from Chrome specifically requires passing device-auth. Bottom line: an open receiver usable by open senders is a weekend-to-modest project on top of openscreen; an open receiver that Chrome/Netflix/YouTube will talk to is effectively blocked by the fused-key cert chain.
transmitterNotes: Transmitter side is much friendlier. The wire protocol for the control channel is well-understood and reimplemented many times; you can build a working sender with pychromecast/node-castv2 in hours, since senders don't need any Google-issued credentials and can skip device-auth verification entirely. For app developers, the official CAF sender SDKs (Android/iOS/Web) hide the protocol and are the normal path; the only friction is registering an app ID in the Cast Developer Console and (for a real product) getting the receiver app approved. Note the mode split: URL-based media casting is simple (send a LOAD with an HLS/DASH/MP4 URL); tab/desktop mirroring from a custom sender is much harder because it needs the RTP/RTCP streaming stack and, against real devices, device-auth from the receiver — most open senders therefore only do URL casting, not mirroring.

contestedClaims.claim: Branding timeline: 'Google Cast' SDK launched 2013/2014, was renamed to 'Chromecast built-in' at the end of 2016, and was renamed back to 'Google Cast' at Google I/O in May 2024.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Multiple secondary sources (9to5Google, Android Central, Wikipedia) agree on the shape, but exact dates wobble (the SDK 'launch' is variously Feb 2014 or mid-2013; the 2016 rename is 'end of 2016'). The device brand 'Chromecast' never went away; only the built-in/licensed-tech label flipped. Commonly conflated by readers.

contestedClaims.claim: Chrome sets enforce_nonce_checking=false, so it accepts replayed device-auth signatures (the basis of the Shanocast bypass).
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Sourced from a single reverse-engineering blog (xakcop/Shanocast). Plausible and consistent with other RE notes, but it's one source about a specific Chrome build; behavior may have changed in later Chrome versions.

contestedClaims.claim: The device private key is fused into the SoC and unreadable, and gen-1 Chromecasts could be rooted to extract keys (Eureka-ROM / gtv-ca-sign).
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Well-attested by Tristan Penman and older RE work, but hardware specifics vary by generation; 'fused, unreadable' is the general design intent rather than a guarantee for every device revision.

contestedClaims.claim: The March 2025 mass Chromecast outage was caused by the gen-2 Intermediate CA certificate expiring (10-year validity from ~2015).
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Widely reported (Register, mobileidworld, Lobsters, Penman) and consistent, but exact cert validity windows and which device generations were affected are reported with minor variation.

contestedClaims.claim: Cast mirroring uses a custom (non-RFC-3550-strict) RTP/RTCP over UDP with Offer/Answer signaling carried over the CASTv2 control channel.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Taken from the openscreen streaming README and RE summaries; the 'custom, not strictly RFC 3550' framing and exact codec/negotiation details are accurate in spirit but I did not verify byte-level conformance, and Google's implementation evolves.

contestedClaims.claim: DIAL was co-developed by Netflix and YouTube and is a separate discovery/app-launch path from mDNS+CASTv2.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Well-documented historically, but how much modern Cast still relies on DIAL vs mDNS (beyond YouTube's specific launch flow) is fuzzy and likely device/app-dependent.

DIAL — legacy discovery + app-launch layer (SSDP-based), still used by e.g. YouTube; distinct from CASTv2
Cast SDK v2 (legacy sender API) vs Cast Application Framework / CAF (current sender+receiver API); Google pushed migration off v2
Web Receiver tiers: Default Media Receiver, Styled Media Receiver, Custom Web Receiver; plus native Android TV Receiver
Two content modes: media-URL casting (receiver fetches HLS/DASH/MP4) vs mirroring/remoting (real-time RTP over UDP)
Brand/tech variants: Chromecast (device) vs Google Cast (SDK/protocol) vs Chromecast built-in / Google Cast (licensed receiver tech in TVs/speakers)
Hardware generations: Chromecast 1/2/3, Chromecast Ultra (4K), Chromecast Audio, Chromecast with Google TV (4K/HD), and the successor Google TV Streamer (2024)
confidence: Medium-high on architecture, discovery/control/media split, and the device-auth blocker (cross-checked across official docs, chromium/openscreen source, and multiple independent RE writeups). Medium on exact dates (branding timeline, cert-expiry specifics) and on single-source RE details like Chrome's nonce-checking flag. Low on any byte-level protocol specifics, which I deliberately did not verify.

name: AirPlay (AirPlay 1 and AirPlay 2)
aka: RAOP (Remote Audio Output Protocol, the audio sub-protocol)
category: screen-mirroring, media-URL-casting (video), audio streaming, multi-room audio (transport substrate spanning several sub-protocols)
summary: AirPlay is Apple's proprietary suite of wireless streaming protocols for sending audio, video, photos, and full screen mirroring from Apple devices (and licensed apps) to receivers like Apple TV, HomePod, and MFi-licensed speakers/TVs. It is not one protocol but a bundle: an RTSP/RTP-based audio path (RAOP/AirTunes), a separate video/AV path that hands off media URLs (HLS/progressive HTTP) to the receiver, and a proprietary mirroring path streaming H.264/HEVC. AirPlay 2 (2018) reworked the stack around HomeKit-style pairing, ChaCha20-Poly1305-encrypted control channels, PTP-based multi-room timing, and buffered audio. Building an open receiver is feasible for audio and mirroring (multiple projects exist) but is gated by pairing/auth crypto and, for commercial certification, Apple's MFi hardware auth chip.
transmitterPlatforms: iOS/iPadOS (native, Control Center + per-app AirPlay picker)
macOS (native screen mirroring, audio, and AV out)
tvOS/Apple TV (can relay/originate)
Third-party iOS/macOS apps via AVFoundation/AVPlayer (external playback) — no low-level SDK exposed; apps hand a media item to the OS which does the AirPlay handoff
Windows via iTunes (AirPlay 1 audio, and limited AirPlay 2)
Open-source transmitters exist but are rarer than receivers (e.g. libraries in pyatv can act as a controller/sender for some paths)
receiverPlatforms: Apple TV (reference receiver, all paths)
HomePod / HomePod mini (audio, AirPlay 2, HomeKit)
MFi-licensed smart TVs (Samsung, LG, Sony, Vizio) and receivers/speakers — audio and often video
Roku devices (AirPlay 2 audio+video via license)
macOS Monterey+ (a Mac can be an AirPlay receiver)
Open-source audio receivers: Shairport / Shairport Sync (AP1 + partial AP2 audio), airplay2-receiver (Python)
Open-source mirroring receivers: RPiPlay, UxPlay, PhairPlay
Embedded ports: shairport-esp32, shairplay-esp32
howItWorks: Discovery: receivers advertise over Bonjour/mDNS. AirPlay 1 uses two service types — _raop._tcp for audio (with a MAC-prefixed instance name) and _airplay._tcp for video/photo/mirroring. Capabilities (codecs, encryption types, feature bitmask) are published in DNS-SD TXT records; a 'features'/'flags' bitmask signals which auth types and media features the receiver supports. AirPlay 2 keeps _airplay._tcp but folds much more into it and adds HomeKit-style attributes. Session setup runs over RTSP (a variant reusing HTTP/1.1-style requests): ANNOUNCE/SETUP/RECORD negotiate an audio session via SDP; the receiver returns UDP ports for the three audio channels (audio data, control/retransmit, timing). Three distinct media paths: (1) AUDIO (RAOP/AirTunes) — RTP over UDP, historically ALAC 44.1kHz/16-bit, also AAC/AAC-ELD/PCM, AES-encrypted payloads with clock sync via NTP (AP1) or PTP (AP2). (2) VIDEO/AV — NOT a pixel stream; the sender POSTs a Content-Location URL (often an HLS playlist or progressive HTTP file) and the receiver fetches and plays it itself, with /play, /scrub, /rate style HTTP control. (3) MIRRORING — a proprietary session on port ~7100 carrying H.264 (AP1) or H.264/HEVC (AP2) NAL units with binary headers and NTP/PTP timestamps; the mirrored audio rides AAC-ELD over the AirTunes path. AirPlay 2 wraps the RTSP control channel in ChaCha20-Poly1305 after pairing and adds separate event and data stream channels with HKDF-derived directional keys.
lowerLevelProtocols: Bonjour / mDNS / DNS-SD (_raop._tcp, _airplay._tcp)
RTSP (proprietary HTTP/1.1-style variant) for session control
RTP over UDP for audio media
RTCP + RFC 2198 redundancy for AP2 buffered audio
SDP for codec/session description
HTTP/1.1 for video URL handoff and mirroring control
HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) and progressive HTTP download for the video/AV path
NTP for A/V clock sync (AirPlay 1)
PTP / IEEE 1588 (AirPlay 2 timing; shairport-sync uses a 'Not Quite PTP' helper on UDP 319/320)
Wi-Fi (infrastructure) and Wi-Fi Direct / AWDL peer-to-peer since 2014-2017
TLV8 encoding for HomeKit-style pairing messages
authEncryption: Two eras. AirPlay 1 ("legacy pairing"): the RTSP ANNOUNCE carried an AES session key for the audio, historically RSA-wrapped with the AirPort Express public key (James Laird extracted the private key in 2011, enabling ShairPort). Legacy auth types include: unencrypted, RSA (later disabled by Apple), FairPlay (SAPv2.5, via /fp-setup), and MFi-SAP (via /auth-setup, exchanging a 1-byte type + 32-byte Curve25519 public key; MFi-SAP encrypts with AES-128-CTR and relies on Apple's authentication IC producing RSA-1024/SHA-1 signatures). AirPlay 2 ("HomeKit pairing", HAP-derived): pair-setup uses SRP-6a (password/PIN-authenticated key exchange) plus Ed25519 long-term identity keys; pair-verify does a Curve25519 ECDH producing a session key; keys are expanded with HKDF-SHA-512 into direction-specific ChaCha20-Poly1305 keys (salts/info like 'Control-Write/Read-Encryption-Key', 'Events-...', 'DataStream-...'), 64-bit counter nonces. Transient pairing: a single pair-setup (M1-M4) with a fixed PIN (3939 on HomePod/HomeKit devices), no pair-verify, giving an ephemeral SRP shared secret used directly as the ChaCha20 key — this is what most open AP2 audio receivers exploit. Optional 'Pair Setup with Auth' layers MFi certificate/RSA-1024/SHA-1 attestation on top. Separately, FairPlay (SAP / 'playfair', currently v3) protects the AirPlay media/session key exchange itself; it is distinct from FairPlay Streaming DRM used to protect Netflix/Apple TV+/iTunes content.

openImplementations.name: Shairport Sync
openImplementations.notes: The de-facto open AirPlay AUDIO receiver for Linux/BSD. Full AirPlay 1; partial AirPlay 2 audio (realtime ALAC + buffered AAC), HomeKit transient/normal pairing, ChaCha20-Poly1305 RTSP, can be added to the Home app. Uses companion NQPTP ('Not Quite PTP', root, UDP 319/320) for AP2 timing/multi-room. Does NOT do video or mirroring; no MFi hardware auth (so it can't be certified).

openImplementations.name: UxPlay
openImplementations.notes: GPLv3 AirPlay 2 MIRRORING + audio receiver for Linux/macOS/BSD. Descends from RPiPlay/AirplayServer/shairplay/playfair. Full pipeline: mDNS, RTSP handshake, HomeKit-style pairing, FairPlay(playfair) key decryption, H.264 1080p + HEVC/4K mirroring, AAC-ELD/AAC-LC/ALAC audio, A/V sync, DACP reverse remote. Uses GStreamer for decode (hardware-accelerated where available). Optional PIN/password/device-ID gating.

openImplementations.name: RPiPlay
openImplementations.maturity: stable but less actively developed (ancestor of UxPlay)
openImplementations.notes: Raspberry Pi AirPlay mirroring receiver. Contains lib/fairplay_playfair.c — the reverse-engineered 'playfair' FairPlay handshake using hardcoded 142-byte reply messages, emulating Apple's fp-setup rather than using a chip.

openImplementations.name: openairplay/airplay2-receiver
openImplementations.notes: Pure-Python AP2 receiver: HomeKit transient + non-transient pairing (SRP/Curve25519/ChaCha20), 'first and only Python FairPlay v3' impl, realtime + buffered audio (ALAC/AAC/OPUS/PCM). Explicitly does NOT do FairPlay v2, accurate PTP sync, or MFi (needs hardware module). Good reference for the shape of the stack.

openImplementations.name: pair_ap
openImplementations.notes: Standalone C implementation of AirPlay/HomeKit pairing (SRP-6a, transient, HomeKit, MFi-SAP, pair-verify). Used as the pairing core by other projects (e.g. owntone). Isolates the crypto handshake.

openImplementations.name: pyatv
openImplementations.notes: Library for controlling Apple TV/AirPlay devices; documents and implements RAOP, AirPlay 2 pairing (legacy + HomeKit), MRP, Companion, DMAP. Primarily a controller/sender but excellent protocol documentation.

openImplementations.name: Unofficial AirPlay Protocol Specification (nto.github.io) + openairplay/airplay-spec + emanuelecozzi.net AirPlay 2 Internals
openImplementations.notes: The three key open documentation efforts. nto covers AP1 thoroughly; openairplay/airplay-spec documents HomeKit pairing (hkp.html) and RTSP requests; Emanuele Cozzi's site documents AP2 internals/authentication (explicitly incomplete).

openImplementations.name: PhairPlay
openImplementations.notes: Ad-free open AirPlay 2 + Miracast + Google Cast receiver — a newer multi-protocol receiver effort; less battle-tested than UxPlay/Shairport Sync.

closedImplementations.name: Apple AirPlay (reference stack in iOS/macOS/tvOS/audioOS)
closedImplementations.licensing: Proprietary, no public SDK for the wire protocol; app-level access only via AVFoundation external playback
closedImplementations.notes: Apple TV and HomePod are the reference receivers implementing every path including FairPlay Streaming DRM content.

closedImplementations.licensing: Requires membership in Apple's MFi Program (NDA, certification, per-unit royalties) and use of the Apple Authentication Coprocessor IC for MFi-SAP attestation

protocolDocs: No official public specification exists for the wire protocol. AirPlay is documented in three overlapping community reverse-engineering efforts: (1) the 'Unofficial AirPlay Protocol Specification' at nto.github.io — strong on AirPlay 1 (RAOP, RTSP, mirroring headers, feature bitmask); (2) openairplay/airplay-spec (GitHub Pages) — HomeKit pairing (hkp.html), RTSP request catalog, auth-setup; (3) Emanuele Cozzi's 'AirPlay 2 Internals' (emanuelecozzi.net) — AP2 authentication, buffered/realtime audio, encryption (explicitly incomplete). Source-code-as-spec: shairport-sync's AIRPLAY2.md, RPiPlay's fairplay_playfair.c, pair_ap, and airplay2-receiver. Apple publishes only high-level marketing docs plus the MFi/HomeKit Accessory Protocol (HAP) spec (under MFi NDA) from which the AP2 pairing was derived. Mirroring internals remain the least fully documented ('not yet fully reverse-engineered' per Wikipedia).
receiverFeasibility: Building an open receiver is demonstrably achievable and the state of the art is good — but feasibility differs sharply by path. AUDIO (AirPlay 1): fully solved (ShairPort et al.) since the AirPort Express RSA key leak. AUDIO (AirPlay 2): solved well enough for real use via HomeKit *transient* pairing (fixed PIN 3939, single SRP exchange, ChaCha20-Poly1305) — no Apple secret needed; shairport-sync + NQPTP handle realtime ALAC and buffered AAC and even multi-room, though accurate PTP timing and full HomeKit integration are the rough edges. MIRRORING: solved by UxPlay/RPiPlay for H.264 and HEVC; the FairPlay 'playfair' handshake that protects the session key was reverse-engineered and is emulated with hardcoded reply messages (no chip). VIDEO/AV: partially solved — receiver just fetches an HLS/HTTP URL, which is easy, EXCEPT when the source app uses FairPlay Streaming DRM (Netflix, Apple TV+, DRM'd iTunes), which an open receiver cannot decrypt. The three real blockers: (a) MFi hardware authentication IC — required only for *certified/commercial* products and for sources that demand MFi-SAP; open receivers sidestep it via transient/HomeKit pairing, so it is not a blocker for hobby/self-use. (b) FairPlay Streaming content DRM — a hard wall for premium video; unrelated to the FairPlay-SAP that protects the AirPlay session (which IS reverse-engineered). (c) Precise PTP multi-room timing and evolving iOS-version quirks (newer iOS releases periodically break open AP2 receivers). Net: an open audio+mirroring receiver for personal use is very feasible; a certified product or one that plays DRM'd streaming video is not.
transmitterNotes: The transmitter (sender/source) side is less reverse-engineered than the receiver side because Apple keeps senders behind the OS: third-party apps cannot speak the AirPlay wire protocol directly, they only mark an AVPlayer item as externally playable and let iOS/macOS perform the handoff. Open sender implementations exist mainly as controllers (pyatv can pair with and command devices, drive RAOP audio out, use MRP/Companion for remote control) and as libraries used to push audio to speakers. Sending to a receiver requires performing the same pairing (legacy RSA/SRP for AP1, HomeKit pair-setup/pair-verify for AP2) and, to reach MFi-only sinks, the MFi-SAP handshake — which again needs the Apple auth chip on the *accessory* side, not necessarily the sender. Sending mirroring/video from a non-Apple platform is comparatively niche and immature. For most integration work, treating Apple devices as the sender and building the receiver is the pragmatic path.

name: DIAL (DIscovery And Launch)
category: app-launch (second-screen app discovery + launch); NOT a media-streaming or screen-mirroring protocol. Acts as a discovery/launch control substrate that app-specific streaming protocols layer on top of.
summary: DIAL is a lightweight LAN protocol that lets a "second screen" (phone, tablet, laptop) discover a "first screen" device (TV, set-top box, Blu-ray player, streaming stick) and remotely launch, query, or stop a named application on it, optionally passing a small text payload. It does exactly two things: SSDP-based discovery and a tiny HTTP/REST app-control API. Crucially it does NOT stream media, mirror screens, or control playback — once DIAL launches (say) the YouTube or Netflix app on the TV, an entirely separate, app-specific and usually proprietary protocol takes over to actually queue and play content. It was authored by Netflix and YouTube (with input from Sony and Samsung) and was the original discovery/launch mechanism inside first-gen Chromecast/Google Cast before Google moved Cast to mDNS plus its own proprietary control protocol.
transmitterPlatforms: Mobile apps (iOS/Android) that embed DIAL client logic — historically the Netflix and YouTube mobile apps used DIAL to find and launch their TV counterparts
Desktop/CLI tools and libraries acting as DIAL clients (e.g. ytcast on the command line)
First-gen Google Cast SDK v1 apps used DIAL under the hood as the sender-side launch mechanism (later superseded)
Any device that can send an SSDP M-SEARCH on the LAN and issue HTTP GET/POST/DELETE — the client side is trivial to implement
receiverPlatforms: Smart TVs and their built-in YouTube/Netflix apps (Samsung, Sony, LG, etc.)
Streaming devices / set-top boxes: Amazon Fire TV (documented DIAL server, integrates via whisperplay.xml), Roku, Android TV / Google TV
First-gen Chromecast (implemented a DIAL-over-SSDP server for Cast SDK v1)
Blu-ray players and other CE devices with embedded streaming apps
Any device running an open DIAL server implementation (pydial, peer-dial, etc.)
howItWorks: Two components. (1) DIAL Service Discovery: the client sends an SSDP M-SEARCH over UDP to multicast 239.255.255.250:1900 with search target ST = urn:dial-multiscreen-org:service:dial:1. A DIAL server responds like a normal UPnP/SSDP device with a LOCATION header pointing to its UPnP device-description XML. The client then HTTP GETs that LOCATION URL; the response is a standard UPnP device description, but with one extra HTTP response header, Application-URL, giving the base URL of the DIAL REST service (commonly on port 8008 for Chromecast, other ports elsewhere). The UPnP friendlyName is used for presenting device choices in the client UI. (2) DIAL REST Service: each app is a resource at {Application-URL}/{AppName}, where AppName is a registered name like "YouTube" or "Netflix". GET returns a small text/xml <service> document reporting state (running / stopped / installable=<url> / hidden) plus an allowStop flag and, when running, a <link rel="run" href="run"> to the app-instance URL. POST launches the app (empty body, or an optional <=4KB text/plain UTF-8 argument passed to the app); on success returns 201 Created with a LOCATION header = the application-instance URL. DELETE on the instance URL stops the app (support is only RECOMMENDED; 501 if unsupported). That is the entire protocol surface. Everything about what the launched app then does — video selection, playback, session control — is out of DIAL's scope. For YouTube specifically, the DIAL app-state's app-specific additionalData carries a screenId, which a client exchanges with YouTube's undocumented Lounge API for a loungeToken that authorizes actual play/pause/queue commands; Netflix similarly hands off to its own protocol.
lowerLevelProtocols: SSDP (Simple Service Discovery Protocol, from UPnP Device Architecture 1.1) over UDP multicast 239.255.255.250:1900 — for discovery
UPnP device description (HTTP GET of an XML description document) — reused, extended only by the Application-URL header
HTTP 1.0 (required) / HTTP 1.1 (recommended), RFC 2616 — for the REST API
text/xml + text/plain payloads (UTF-8)
Wake-on-LAN, optional, in later spec versions (2.x) via a WAKEUP hint header so a sleeping TV can be woken before launch
authEncryption: The base spec (v1.6.4) has essentially NO auth, NO pairing, and NO encryption: it explicitly states the protocol works without requiring any pairing between devices, and all traffic is plaintext HTTP on the LAN. Any DIAL client on the same subnet can launch/stop registered apps. The trust boundary is "you're on the LAN." Security is deliberately pushed up to (a) the launched app and (b) later spec revisions. The DIAL payload MUST NOT be usable to subvert platform integrity (no command-line injection, no arbitrary executable naming). Real authentication is entirely app-specific and happens AFTER launch: e.g. YouTube's screenId -> Lounge loungeToken exchange, or an out-of-band "link with TV code" pairing for devices not reachable by DIAL; Netflix uses its own login/session handoff. Later spec versions (2.1/2.2/2.2.1) added CORS controls so a browser-based second-screen app must be an authorized origin (Fire TV exposes this as <authorizedOrigins> in whisperplay.xml, wildcard "*" allowed, insecure file:/http:/ftp: origins forbidden), and an additionalDataUrl mechanism so the first-screen app can publish extra data (like the screenId) to the client. There is no DRM in DIAL itself; DRM lives inside the streaming apps DIAL launches (e.g. Widevine/PlayReady in Netflix/YouTube).

protocolDocs: Official and public. The canonical text is the "DIAL DIscovery And Launch protocol specification" — v1.6.4 is Copyright 2012 Netflix, Inc. and is freely redistributable under a BSD-style permissive license (the DIAL word mark itself is trademarked by Netflix, licensing info at dial-multiscreen.org). Later revisions (2.1, 2.2 released Oct 29 2018, 2.2.1 released Sep 4 2020) are published at dial-multiscreen.org and add additionalDataUrl, WAKEUP/wake-on-LAN hints, and tighter CORS/security rules. Supporting docs: Amazon Fire TV DIAL integration guide (concrete server-side reference), UPnP Device Architecture 1.1, RFC 2616 (HTTP), RFC 3986 (URI/app-name pchar rules). Reverse-engineering writeups exist mainly for the app-specific layers that ride ON TOP of DIAL (YouTube Lounge API teardowns, OakBits Google Cast protocol series) rather than DIAL itself, since DIAL is openly specified.
receiverFeasibility: Building an open DIAL RECEIVER (sink) is genuinely easy — this is one of the lowest-effort protocols to implement. Requirements: (1) answer SSDP M-SEARCH for ST=urn:dial-multiscreen-org:service:dial:1 with a LOCATION header; (2) serve a UPnP device-description XML with an added Application-URL header (and a friendlyName); (3) implement the REST endpoints: GET {base}/{App} returning the tiny <service> state XML, POST to launch (return 201 + LOCATION instance URL), DELETE to stop. No auth chip, no DRM, no license, no certification is needed to stand up the DIAL layer itself; pydial/peer-dial prove a full server is a few hundred lines. THE REAL BLOCKERS ARE NOT IN DIAL — they are in what a launched app must then do to be useful: (a) to have a real 'YouTube' or 'Netflix' app respond, you need the actual (closed, certified) TV app installed and reachable, and the registered app name from the DIAL Registry; (b) the post-launch control/streaming protocol is app-specific and mostly proprietary/undocumented (YouTube Lounge is reverse-engineered and fragile; Netflix's is closed); (c) content playback pulls in DRM (Widevine/PlayReady) which requires licensing. So: an open DIAL receiver that advertises and launches arbitrary named apps is trivial; an open receiver that convincingly impersonates YouTube/Netflix to real sender apps and then actually plays their content is blocked by app registration, undocumented control protocols, and DRM — not by DIAL. This is exactly why leapcast worked briefly then died when Google moved on.
transmitterNotes: Transmitter (sender/client) side is even simpler than the receiver: send an SSDP M-SEARCH, GET the LOCATION to read Application-URL and friendlyName, then GET/POST/DELETE against {Application-URL}/{AppName}. No pairing, no crypto required at the DIAL layer. The catch is the same asymmetry: launching is trivial, but doing anything meaningful after launch means implementing the target app's proprietary control layer. ytcast is the clearest example — DIAL to discover+launch YouTube, then the reverse-engineered Lounge API (screenId -> loungeToken) to queue/play/pause. A transmitter that only needs to power-on-and-launch a known app (e.g. home-automation 'open Netflix on the TV') is straightforward and robust; a transmitter that wants full remote control inherits fragility from undocumented app protocols that can change without notice.
variants: v1.6.4 (2012, Copyright Netflix) — the widely cited baseline: SSDP discovery, Application-URL header, GET/POST/DELETE REST, states running/stopped/installable=/hidden, allowStop, <link rel=run>, DIAL Registry for app names, no auth/pairing
v2.1 — introduced additionalData / additionalDataUrl so first-screen apps can expose app-specific data (e.g. YouTube screenId) to clients
v2.2 (released 2018-10-29) — further additionalData formatting, wake-on-LAN / WAKEUP capability hint, refined security
v2.2.1 (released 2020-09-04) — further closure of CORS security gaps for browser-based second-screen apps

name: Miracast (Wi-Fi CERTIFIED Miracast / Wi-Fi Display) and Intel WiDi
category: screen-mirroring (wireless display mirroring; also supports non-mirror "direct streaming" of media in R2)
summary: Miracast is the Wi-Fi Alliance's certification brand for its "Wi-Fi Display" (WFD) specification: a peer-to-peer wireless display standard that behaves like a "wireless HDMI cable," mirroring a source device's screen and audio to a sink (receiver). A source encodes the screen as H.264 (optionally HEVC), packages it as an MPEG2-TS elementary stream, and streams it over RTP/UDP to the sink; an RTSP control channel negotiates capabilities and controls the session. The link itself is a direct Wi-Fi Direct (P2P) connection secured by WPS/WPA2, not a route through an access point. Intel WiDi (Wireless Display) was Intel's earlier proprietary predecessor/superset technology that eventually became a Miracast-compatible implementation before Intel discontinued it in favor of native OS Miracast support.
aka: Intel WiDi / Intel Wireless Display (predecessor implementation)
transmitterPlatforms: Windows: native source since Windows 8.1; Windows 10/11 project via Win+K ('Connect to a wireless display' / 'Cast'). Uses the OS Miracast source stack over the Wi-Fi driver.

Android: native source ('Cast'/'Smart View'/'Wireless projection') from Android 4.2 through ~5.x. Google removed the generic Miracast API in Android 6.0 (2015) in favor of Google Cast, though many OEMs (Samsung, etc.) kept vendor Miracast source stacks.
Intel WiDi: shipped as a Windows source application (v3.5-6.0 were Miracast-compatible) tied to Intel Wi-Fi + GPU; discontinued 2015-2016.
Linux (open-source source/transmitter): GNOME Network Displays and MiracleCast can act as a source, riding wpa_supplicant P2P + GStreamer; maturity is variable.
Miracast source SDKs/stacks are typically part of the Wi-Fi chipset/driver vendor's software (Broadcom, Qualcomm/Atheros, Intel, Realtek, MediaTek).
receiverPlatforms: Windows 10/11 PCs: the built-in 'Wireless Display'/'Connect' app turns the PC into a Miracast sink. Since Windows 10 v2004 it is an on-demand Optional Feature (not installed by default); on Windows 11 it is the 'Wireless Display' optional feature (installable via Settings > Optional features, or DISM/PowerShell).

Dedicated hardware sink dongles/adapters: Microsoft Wireless Display Adapter, Actiontec ScreenBeam, EZCast, AnyCast, Netgear Push2TV (originally a WiDi adapter), and many generic 'AnyCast/MiraScreen' dongles.
Smart TVs and set-top boxes: many TVs (Samsung, LG, Sony, etc.) and streaming boxes ship a Miracast sink, often branded 'Screen Mirroring'.
Android devices historically could act as a sink on some OEM builds, but generic sink support was never guaranteed and is uncommon.
Linux (open-source sink): MiracleCast (miracle-sinkctl) and intel/wds sink example implement the sink role on wpa_supplicant P2P + GStreamer, but without HDCP.
howItWorks: "Discovery: devices advertise a WFD Information Element (WFD IE) carrying a 'WFD Device Information' subelement (source/primary-sink/secondary-sink role, availability, preferred control port) inside 802.11 Probe Request/Response and P2P/service-discovery frames. R1 uses Wi-Fi Direct service/device discovery; R2 adds discovery that can also work over an infrastructure BSS. Connection: the two peers form a Wi-Fi Direct P2P group (one becomes Group Owner) and pair/provision the link with WPS, yielding a WPA2-secured direct link; the sink gets an IP via a lightweight DHCP exchange. TDLS is an alternative transport when both devices are already on the same infrastructure AP. Session setup: over TCP (default control port 7236) the source and sink run an RTSP dialect (the M1-M7+ message sequence): OPTIONS/capability exchange (GET/SET_PARAMETER, method M3/M4) negotiates resolutions, codecs, profiles/levels, audio formats, and content-protection support, then SETUP/PLAY (M6/M7) starts streaming. Streaming: the source captures/encodes screen video as H.264 (or optional HEVC) plus audio, multiplexes them into an MPEG2 Transport Stream, and sends TS packets inside RTP over UDP to the sink, which demuxes, decodes, and renders. RTSP continues to carry control (pause, resume, standby, resolution/level changes, optional UIBC user-input back-channel). If HDCP 2.x is in play, a separate TCP connection carries HDCP AKE/locality-check/SKE and the media PES payloads are encrypted."
lowerLevelProtocols: Wi-Fi Direct (Wi-Fi P2P) as the primary link/transport
IEEE 802.11 (a/g/n/ac; WiGig/802.11ad in some high-rate variants)
TDLS (Tunneled Direct Link Setup) as an optional alternate transport over an existing BSS
WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) for pairing/provisioning
WPA2 for link encryption
IPv4 + DHCP (lightweight) for addressing
RTSP (WFD-specific dialect) for control plane, over TCP (default port 7236)
RTP over UDP for media transport (optional RTCP; R2 can fall back to RTP over TCP)
MPEG2-TS (H.222) container for the A/V elementary streams
H.264/AVC (mandatory video), H.265/HEVC (optional)
LPCM (mandatory audio), AAC / AC-3 / E-AC-3 (optional audio)
HDCP 2.x (interface-independent adaptation) for link content protection
authEncryption: "Pairing/link: WPS provisions the Wi-Fi Direct group, and the resulting P2P link is encrypted with WPA2 (AES-CCMP). This protects the link but is unrelated to premium-content DRM. Content protection: Miracast uses HDCP 2.x (2.0/2.1/2.2, the interface-independent 'wireless' adaptation of HDCP) as an OPTIONAL capability. Key nuance from the spec: HDCP is only invoked/required when the source wants to send content that is subject to link-content-protection (protected/premium content). If both source and sink advertise HDCP support (via the wfd-content-protection RTSP parameter), they MUST complete HDCP AKE + locality check + Session Key Exchange (SKE) before any RTP streaming; HDCP-protected PES video payloads are then AES-encrypted. If the sink does not support HDCP (or the SKE fails), the source may still stream, but only unprotected content. HDCP messaging runs on a separate TCP connection from RTSP, with the sink acting as the HDCP/TCP server. Building an HDCP-capable receiver requires per-device HDCP production keys licensed from Digital Content Protection LLC (DCP), plus conformance to HDCP robustness rules — this is the principal DRM blocker for open receivers."

Early versions predated Miracast and used Intel-specific source+sink pairing (e.g., Netgear Push2TV adapters); v3.5-6.0 became Miracast-compatible. Discontinued: Intel stopped marketing/dev in Oct 2015 and ended development ~2016, redirecting users to OS-native Miracast.
closedImplementations.licensing: Proprietary Intel; required Intel Wi-Fi + Intel GPU + WiDi software. Now discontinued.

closedImplementations.name: ScreenBeam (Actiontec), Microsoft Wireless Display Adapter, EZCast/AnyCast/MiraScreen dongles, Push2TV
closedImplementations.notes: Commercial hardware Miracast sinks. ScreenBeam is a common enterprise-grade certified receiver; the cheap 'AnyCast' class dongles are variable-quality generic sinks. These embed licensed chipset firmware and (for premium content) HDCP keys.
closedImplementations.licensing: Vendor firmware; Wi-Fi Alliance Miracast certification + (if HDCP) DCP HDCP keys.

closedImplementations.name: Smart TV / STB vendor Miracast sinks (Samsung, LG, Sony, etc.)
closedImplementations.notes: 'Screen Mirroring' features are vendor closed-source Miracast sink stacks integrated with the TV's SoC media pipeline and HDCP.
closedImplementations.licensing: Per-vendor; typically Miracast-certified with licensed HDCP.

protocolDocs: "official/public. The core spec is publicly downloadable from the Wi-Fi Alliance: 'Wi-Fi Display Technical Specification' (Miracast), current at v2.3 (2024) — this is the primary source and it is unusually open for a certification-body spec. A public 'Wi-Fi CERTIFIED Miracast Technical Overview' whitepaper also exists. HOWEVER, two things are gated: (1) the full certification test plans and the right to use the Miracast brand require Wi-Fi Alliance membership; (2) HDCP 2.x itself is specified by DCP LLC — the HDCP spec is public, but production device keys and the license are NDA/paid. Reverse-engineering/reference writeups: intel/wds (archived) and MiracleCast are the best code-level references for the RTSP dialect and negotiation; various blog/teardown writeups (e.g., sudonull, HandWiki, GStreamer bug threads) cover the RTP/MPEG-TS framing."
receiverFeasibility: "Building an open UNPROTECTED-content sink is very feasible and already exists (MiracleCast, intel/wds sink). The architecture is well-understood: (1) a Wi-Fi Direct P2P stack via wpa_supplicant compiled with CONFIG_P2P (this is the hardest OS-integration piece — driver/firmware P2P support and Group-Owner behavior are the usual source of pain and flaky pairing), (2) WPS/WPA2 provisioning, (3) a small DHCP server, (4) an RTSP server implementing the WFD M1-M7 dialect and capability negotiation, and (5) a GStreamer/FFmpeg pipeline to demux MPEG2-TS, decode H.264/HEVC, and render + play LPCM/AAC audio. The BLOCKERS for a fully-compliant sink are: (a) HDCP 2.x — receiving premium/DRM-protected streams requires licensed HDCP device keys from DCP LLC and robustness compliance; you cannot legally/open-source clone this, so open sinks simply advertise no HDCP and are limited to unprotected content (which covers general screen-mirroring but not Netflix/Blu-ray-class content, and can break interop with sources that insist on HDCP2.x like some Windows configs). (b) The Miracast brand/logo requires Wi-Fi Alliance certification and membership. (c) Real-world interop quirks with Windows 11 / modern Android sources (P2P negotiation, resolution/level handshakes) are the practical time sink. Net: an open 'mirror my laptop screen' receiver is a weekend-to-months project on the right hardware; an open 'plays protected streaming content' receiver is effectively impossible without a DCP HDCP license."
transmitterNotes: "Transmitter (source) side is also feasible openly and exists (GNOME Network Displays as source; MiracleCast/intel/wds source paths). The source needs the same P2P+WPS+RTSP plumbing plus a screen-capture/encode pipeline (H.264, optionally HEVC) that muxes to MPEG2-TS/RTP. The source is the HDCP transmitter role: to send protected content it would need HDCP keys, but a general screen-mirroring source can operate without HDCP just fine. Practical friction mirrors the sink: reliable Wi-Fi Direct via wpa_supplicant, and encoder latency/quality tuning. On commodity OSes the source is usually already provided natively (Windows Win+K, Android Cast/Smart View), so open source-side work mostly matters on Linux."
variants: Miracast R1 (Release 1): original 2012 spec — Wi-Fi Direct or TDLS transport, H.264 video, mandatory LPCM audio; up to 1080p.

Miracast R2 (Release 2): adds HEVC/H.265, 4K (3840x2160), 'direct streaming' of media (URL/file handoff, auxiliary streams like subtitles/captions), coupled-sink operation (separate audio sink), discovery over an infrastructure BSS, and RTP-over-TCP fallback. Public Miracast Specification versions track to ~v2.1 (2017, added 4K) through v2.3 (2024).

Miracast over Infrastructure (MS-MICE): a Microsoft extension letting Miracast run over an existing LAN/Wi-Fi infrastructure network instead of a direct P2P link (used in enterprise/education); complements, not replaces, standard P2P Miracast.
WiGig-based / 802.11ad high-rate variant for very high bandwidth (uncompressed-ish/low-latency) — niche.
Intel WiDi generations: pre-Miracast proprietary (v1-v3) vs Miracast-compatible (v3.5-6.0); plus Intel Pro WiDi enterprise variant.

contestedClaims.claim: HDCP is mandatory for all Miracast devices.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: This is commonly misreported. Per the WFD spec, HDCP 2.x is an OPTIONAL capability that is only required WHEN transmitting protected/premium content and only when both peers support it. Unprotected screen mirroring does not require HDCP. Certification tests HDCP when the device claims it, and some SOURCES (certain Windows configs, streaming apps) refuse to stream without it, which blurs the 'optional' line in practice — but it is not a blanket mandatory feature.

contestedClaims.claim: Intel WiDi 'is' Miracast / WiDi and Miracast are the same thing.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Nuanced: early WiDi (pre-2013) was Intel-proprietary and NOT Miracast; only WiDi ~v3.5+ became Miracast-compatible. WiDi was an implementation/brand, Miracast is the WFA standard. Many sources conflate them or imply WiDi simply 'became' Miracast, which understates the earlier proprietary phase.

contestedClaims.claim: Miracast uses H.264 over 'RTP' directly (no MPEG-TS), or conversely never uses TS.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Frequently oversimplified. The spec muxes A/V into an MPEG2 Transport Stream, which is then carried in RTP/UDP. Some summaries drop the TS layer or the RTP layer. Confidence is high from the primary spec, but casual sources describe it inconsistently.

contestedClaims.claim: Exact Miracast version that first added HEVC/4K.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Sources attribute 4K/HEVC to 'Miracast R2' and to public spec 'v2.1 (2017)'. The R-release vs public-spec-version numbering are different axes and are easy to mismatch; I'm confident 4K/HEVC = R2 era but less certain about mapping to a precise dotted spec version.

contestedClaims.claim: Android still supports Miracast natively.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Google removed the generic platform Miracast API in Android 6.0 (2015) in favor of Google Cast, but many OEMs (Samsung Smart View, etc.) retained vendor Miracast source stacks, and behavior varies widely by device/OEM/year. Blanket statements either way are wrong.

contestedClaims.claim: The full Miracast spec is freely public.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: The technical specification PDF is publicly downloadable (v2.3), which is unusual — but the certification test plans, brand usage, and HDCP device keys are gated behind WFA membership and DCP licensing, so 'open spec' should not be read as 'fully open to certify/DRM'.

confidence: high on architecture, transport stack, HDCP role/blocker, and open-implementation landscape (cross-checked against the primary Wi-Fi Alliance WFD spec v2.3, Wikipedia, Microsoft Learn, Intel notices, and the MiracleCast/intel/wds/GNOME repos); medium on precise spec-version-to-feature mappings (R-release vs dotted version) and on current per-OEM Android support details.

name: DLNA / UPnP AV
category: media-URL-casting / media-library-sharing (LAN); UPnP AV is the control substrate, DLNA is an interoperability profile layered on top. Sub-categories: app-launch-style "push" (SetAVTransportURI to a renderer) and library browse/pull (ContentDirectory).
summary: UPnP AV is a set of UPnP device/service definitions for discovering, browsing, and controlling networked media on a LAN. It splits the world into a MediaServer (holds/serves content), a MediaRenderer (plays content), and a ControlPoint (the brains that discovers devices and orchestrates playback via SOAP). DLNA is a now-dissolved industry consortium's interoperability certification and guidelines layered on top of UPnP AV — it pins down mandatory media formats (DIDL-Lite profiles), HTTP streaming rules, and optional DTCP-IP link protection so that certified devices actually interoperate, whereas raw UPnP AV is far more permissive and inconsistently implemented. The actual media bytes almost always travel out-of-band over plain HTTP (renderer GETs from server); the UPnP/SOAP layer is only control and metadata.
variants: Raw UPnP AV (uncertified): UPnP Forum / Open Connectivity Foundation (OCF) DCPs. AVArchitecture v1 (2002) and v2 (2010/2013). Service versions e.g. ContentDirectory:1-4, AVTransport:1-3, RenderingControl:1-3, ConnectionManager:1-3.

DLNA Certified (the interoperability profile): DLNA Guidelines v1.0 (~2004, ~50 media profiles) through v1.5+ (~250 profiles). Adds mandatory HTTP transport, media format profiles, DIDL-Lite constraints, and optional DTCP-IP.

DLNA device classes: DMS (server), DMR (renderer, controlled/pushed to), DMP (player = control-point + renderer that pulls itself), DMC (controller), DMPr (printer), DMU/DMD (uploader/downloader), plus Mobile M-* variants and Media Interoperability Unit / connectivity functions.
UPnP AV '2-box' (server+renderer, control-point integrated) vs '3-box' (separate server, renderer, control point) topology model — a different axis from DLNA's DMR/DMP labels.
OpenHome (Linn) — a separate, non-DLNA control/streaming stack sometimes bolted onto the same renderers (e.g. gmrender-resurrect-openhome fork).
DTCP-IP / DTCP2 — the link-protection variants used by DLNA for protected commercial content.
transmitterPlatforms: Windows: built-in 'Play To' / 'Cast to Device' (Windows Media Player acts as DMC/DMS pushing to a DMR).
Android: many apps embed control-point + server (BubbleUPnP, AllCast, Hi-Fi Cast); Android itself has no first-class OS-level DLNA sender API.
Linux/embedded: Rygel, Gerbera (servers); MPD with UPnP output; BubbleUPnP Server; VLC (uses libupnp) can browse/serve.
NAS boxes (Synology, QNAP, etc.) ship DMS software as transmitter/source.
Mobile handhelds and set-top boxes acting as DMC to orchestrate a separate renderer.
Any app linking libupnp (pupnp) or GUPnP as a control point / MediaServer.
receiverPlatforms: Smart TVs, AV receivers, game consoles (historically PS3/PS4, Xbox) as DMR/DMP sinks.
Linux/embedded via gmrender-resurrect (gmediarender) — headless MediaRenderer on Raspberry Pi etc.
Rygel can also act as a MediaRenderer (GUPnP-based).
Network audio streamers / AV gear (many use OpenHome or DLNA DMR firmware).
Home Assistant 'dlna_dmr' integration controls DMR sinks; PRO-2684/dlna-dmr and similar hobby projects implement a DMR.
Any device linking libupnp/GUPnP plus a media engine (GStreamer) can present as a MediaRenderer.
howItWorks: Discovery: devices announce and are found via SSDP (HTTP-over-UDP multicast to 239.255.255.250:1900) using NOTIFY/M-SEARCH. Description: the control point fetches an XML device description document over HTTP, which lists device type (MediaServer/MediaRenderer), embedded services, and their control/event/SCPD URLs. Control: the control point invokes actions via SOAP (HTTP POST, XML envelope) against each service's control URL. Eventing: state changes are pushed to subscribers via GENA (UPnP's SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY eventing). Content model: a MediaServer exposes a hierarchy through the ContentDirectory service; the control point calls Browse()/Search() and gets back DIDL-Lite XML (Dublin Core + UPnP metadata) describing items, their upnp:class, and one or more <res> resource URLs with protocolInfo (e.g. http-get:*:audio/mpeg:DLNA.ORG_PN=...). Playback (push/DMR path): control point calls AVTransport::SetAVTransportURI(instanceID, uri, metadata) on the renderer, then Play()/Pause()/Stop()/Seek(); RenderingControl handles volume/mute/brightness. Playback (pull/DMP path): the same device is both control point and renderer and drives itself. Media transfer: crucially, the actual bytes are out-of-band — the renderer does an HTTP GET on the <res> URL directly from the server (async pull). ConnectionManager negotiates/inventories transfer capabilities (GetProtocolInfo, PrepareForConnection) but is often thinly implemented. So SOAP is a thin RPC control plane; the data plane is ordinary HTTP (or RTP for some legacy/isochronous cases).
lowerLevelProtocols: SSDP (Simple Service Discovery Protocol) over UDP multicast 239.255.255.250:1900
HTTPU/HTTPMU (HTTP syntax over UDP) for SSDP
HTTP/1.0-1.1 (TCP) for device/service description, SOAP control, and media transfer
SOAP (XML-RPC-style) for action invocation
GENA (General Event Notification Architecture) for eventing (SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY)
XML — device descriptions, SCPD service descriptions, DIDL-Lite content metadata
DIDL-Lite (Dublin Core + UPnP AV vocabulary) content metadata schema
HTTP GET with DLNA range/timeseek headers (getcontentFeatures.dlna.org, transferMode.dlna.org) for DLNA streaming
RTP/RTSP and IEEE-1394 (FireWire) isochronous transport in some legacy/2-box variants
DTCP-IP / DTCP2 as an optional encryption/link-protection layer over the HTTP media stream
authEncryption: Baseline UPnP AV / DLNA has essentially NO authentication and NO transport encryption — discovery, control, and media transfer are all cleartext on the trusted LAN. Anyone on the LAN can browse a MediaServer and control a MediaRenderer. Access control, if any, is out of scope of the base protocol (some servers add IP allowlists). The only real DRM/link-protection is DTCP-IP (Digital Transmission Content Protection over IP), administered by the DTLA (Digital Transmission Licensing Administrator, the '5C' companies: Intel, Sony, Hitachi, Matsushita/Panasonic, Toshiba). DTCP-IP is optional in DLNA and used only for copy-protected commercial content ('link protection' independent of the CA/DRM the content arrived under). Technically DTCP-IP performs an Authentication and Key Exchange (AKE) using elliptic-curve crypto (EC-DSA / EC-DH) with device certificates, then encrypts the content stream with AES (DTCP2 strengthens the crypto). Critically, DTCP relies on 'Highly Confidential' constants/algorithms and device keys/certificates that are only issued to signed DTLA Adopter Agreement licensees — this is the hard blocker for open receivers of protected content.

openImplementations.name: gmrender-resurrect (gmediarender)
openImplementations.notes: Headless MediaRenderer (DMR): implements AVTransport, RenderingControl, ConnectionManager. Built on libupnp (pupnp) for the UPnP stack and GStreamer 1.x for actual decode/playback — so format support == whatever GStreamer plugins are installed. The canonical 'build an open sink on a Raspberry Pi' reference. No DTCP-IP (cleartext content only).

openImplementations.name: Rygel
openImplementations.notes: Primarily a MediaServer but can also act as a MediaRenderer. Built on GUPnP/GUPnP-AV (GObject-based UPnP stack, an alternative to libupnp). Pluggable backends; commonly paired with GStreamer. Good reference for the server/transmitter side and for a GUPnP-based renderer.

openImplementations.name: Gerbera
openImplementations.notes: The maintained fork of the discontinued MediaTomb (0.12.1 base). Full MediaServer (DMS): ContentDirectory browse/search, metadata extraction, thumbnailing, transcoding, web UI. Uses libupnp. This is the go-to open DMS.

openImplementations.name: MediaTomb
openImplementations.notes: Original open UPnP MediaServer; historically important, now effectively replaced by Gerbera.

openImplementations.name: libupnp / pupnp (Portable SDK for UPnP Devices)
openImplementations.notes: The most widely used low-level UPnP stack: SSDP, HTTP, SOAP, GENA for control points, devices, and bridges. Underpins gmrender-resurrect, MPD's UPnP support, VLC's UPnP discovery, and much more. Does the protocol plumbing but not the AV semantics.

openImplementations.name: GUPnP / GUPnP-AV
openImplementations.notes: Alternative GObject-based UPnP stack; GUPnP-AV adds DIDL-Lite parsing/generation and AV helpers. Basis for Rygel.

openImplementations.name: MPD (Music Player Daemon) + upmpdcli
openImplementations.notes: upmpdcli turns MPD into a UPnP/OpenHome MediaRenderer (sink) and can also front UPnP MediaServers; another practical open receiver path.

openImplementations.name: BubbleUPnP Server
openImplementations.maturity: Mature (server is free; Android app is proprietary)
openImplementations.notes: Bridging/control tooling; the Android app is a popular closed control point but the server component is freely available.

closedImplementations.name: DTCP-IP / DTCP2 (DTLA)
closedImplementations.notes: The link-protection/DRM layer. Uses EC-DSA/EC-DH AKE + AES. Depends on confidential constants and device certificates/keys issued only to licensees. This is the single biggest closed blocker for receiving protected commercial content.
closedImplementations.licensing: DTLA (Digital Transmission Licensing Administrator, the '5C' consortium). Requires signing an Adopter Agreement, NDA, per-device certificate/key provisioning, and robustness/compliance rules. Fees + NDA; no open-source implementation is possible without violating the license.

closedImplementations.name: DLNA Certification
closedImplementations.notes: The interoperability testing/branding program. Certification proves a device follows the DLNA Guidelines (formats, HTTP transport, DIDL-Lite constraints). You can build a fully interoperable device without certifying; you just can't use the DLNA logo/claim.
closedImplementations.licensing: Originally DLNA (consortium). Since the org dissolved (Jan 2017, effective transition Feb 1 2017), certification is run by SpireSpark International (Portland, OR), staffed by ex-DLNA people. Now open to any company, no membership required; paid testing program.

closedImplementations.name: Vendor DMS/DMR firmware
closedImplementations.notes: Smart-TV, AV-receiver, and NAS DLNA stacks (Samsung/LG/Sony TVs, Denon/Marantz/Yamaha receivers, Synology/QNAP DiskStation Media Server). Proprietary, often quirky/non-conformant, and the source of most real-world interop pain.
closedImplementations.licensing: Vendor-proprietary; many were DLNA-certified.

closedImplementations.name: Microsoft 'Play To' / Windows Media Player DLNA
closedImplementations.notes: Windows' built-in DMC/DMS/DMR support. Proprietary implementation of the standard protocols; documented partly via MS-DLNHND open-spec.
closedImplementations.licensing: Part of Windows; not separately licensed.

protocolDocs: Mixed but favorable for the base protocols. The UPnP Device Architecture and the UPnP AV DCPs (AVArchitecture v1/v2, and the ContentDirectory / AVTransport / RenderingControl / ConnectionManager service templates) are PUBLIC specifications — originally from the UPnP Forum, now hosted by the Open Connectivity Foundation (OCF) at openconnectivity.org / upnp.org. DIDL-Lite, SSDP, SOAP, and GENA are likewise openly documented. So an open control plane + renderer is fully spec-supported. The DLNA Guidelines themselves (exact media profiles, DLNA.ORG_PN flags, HTTP header rules) were membership/paywalled and are only partly reconstructable from public sources, MS-DLNHND open specs, and reverse-engineering writeups; DLNA test tools require SpireSpark. DTCP-IP/DTCP2 specs are LICENSED-UNDER-NDA (public 'informational' overviews exist at dtcp.com, but the normative crypto details and keys are confidential). Net: base UPnP AV = official/public; DLNA profiling = semi-public/reconstructed; DTCP-IP = NDA/closed.
receiverFeasibility: Building an open MediaRenderer (sink) for UNPROTECTED content is very tractable and already solved — gmrender-resurrect is the existence proof (libupnp for the UPnP plumbing + GStreamer for decode, a few thousand lines of C). The receiver's job is: (1) announce itself as urn:schemas-upnp-org:device:MediaRenderer via SSDP; (2) serve device + SCPD XML over HTTP; (3) implement AVTransport (SetAVTransportURI, Play/Pause/Stop/Seek, GetPositionInfo/GetTransportInfo), RenderingControl (volume/mute), and a minimal ConnectionManager (GetProtocolInfo advertising supported formats); (4) emit GENA events for state changes; (5) HTTP-GET the media URL and feed a decoder. The realistic hard parts are NOT crypto but conformance and interop: correct GENA eventing (LastChange), correct DIDL-Lite metadata handling, honoring DLNA HTTP headers (getcontentFeatures.dlna.org, transferMode.dlna.org, timeseek/range), advertising the right DLNA.ORG_PN profile flags so finicky senders will talk to you, and codec/container coverage (delegated to GStreamer). The ONE genuine blocker is DTCP-IP: any content a server will only release over a DTCP-IP-protected link cannot be received by an open renderer, because DTCP requires DTLA-licensed keys/certificates and confidential algorithms. In practice most home/NAS content is unprotected, so an open sink works for the vast majority of real use; only broadcast/commercial protected streams are off-limits.
transmitterNotes: Transmitter side splits into two roles that are often conflated. (a) MediaServer/DMS (the content source): implement ContentDirectory (Browse/Search returning DIDL-Lite), ConnectionManager, an HTTP file server for the <res> URLs, and SSDP announcements. This is well-trodden — Gerbera and Rygel are mature, and libupnp/GUPnP handle the plumbing. Feasibility is high. (b) ControlPoint/DMC (the orchestrator/'caster'): pure client code — no device to host — that discovers servers and renderers, browses the server, then pushes SetAVTransportURI + Play to the renderer. Also straightforward with libupnp/GUPnP. The 'push' UX (Windows Play To, Android cast apps) is a DMC + DMS combination pointing a DMR at a URL the DMS serves. Note the media bytes still flow server->renderer over HTTP; the controller only sends control. No DTLA licensing is needed to transmit UNPROTECTED content. Transmitting protected content (acting as a DTCP-IP source) would itself require DTLA licensing, so open transmitters are also limited to cleartext.

contestedClaims.claim: 'Push' means the server pushes media bytes to the renderer. In DLNA/UPnP the 'push' (DMR) model means the CONTROLLER pushes a content URI to the renderer via SetAVTransportURI; the renderer then still PULLS the actual bytes via HTTP GET from the server. The 'push/pull' distinction is about control flow (who initiates and who browses), not about which node originates the media stream.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: This is the single most commonly misreported point. Search summaries themselves conflate DLNA's DMR='push'/DMP='pull' labels with UPnP AV's '2-box (isochronous push, e.g. IEEE-1394) vs 3-box (async HTTP pull)' topology model — these are two different axes. I'm confident the media bytes are HTTP-pulled by the renderer in the normal HTTP case, but the exact terminology mapping deserves independent verification against AVArchitecture v1/v2.

contestedClaims.claim: DMR vs DMP distinction: a DMR is a passive renderer that must be driven by an external controller (DMC) and does not browse servers itself; a DMP is a control-point+renderer that discovers and browses servers and drives itself.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Well supported across sources, but devices frequently implement both roles simultaneously, so real-world behavior blurs the clean taxonomy. Worth confirming the precise DLNA guideline definitions.

contestedClaims.claim: DTCP-IP is OPTIONAL in DLNA and only applies to protected commercial content; the vast majority of DLNA/UPnP AV traffic (home media, NAS) is unencrypted with no auth.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Consistent across sources, but the exact set of DLNA guideline versions/profiles in which DTCP-IP became conditionally mandatory (e.g. for certain 'commercial content' or CVP-2 profiles) is fuzzy and I did not pin it to a primary guideline document.

contestedClaims.claim: The DLNA organization dissolved on ~Jan 5, 2017 and certification transitioned to SpireSpark International effective Feb 1, 2017, now open to non-members.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Well cross-checked (DLNA.org, SpireSpark, trade press). Minor uncertainty only on exact dates and whether dlna.org content is still authoritative post-dissolution.

contestedClaims.claim: Media format profiles: DLNA v1.0 ~50 profiles growing to ~250 in later guideline versions.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Numbers come from a Wikipedia-derived summary; the precise counts per guideline version are approximate and not verified against primary DLNA guideline docs (which are paywalled).

contestedClaims.claim: Base UPnP AV specs are public via OCF/upnp.org, but DTCP-IP normative specs are NDA-only.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Confident on both ends; slight uncertainty on exactly which UPnP AV service-template revisions remain freely downloadable after the OCF migration, since some upnp.org PDF links are inconsistent.

confidence: High on the overall architecture (device/service model, SSDP/SOAP/GENA/DIDL-Lite control plane, HTTP out-of-band data plane), on the open-implementation landscape (gmrender-resurrect + libupnp + GStreamer for receivers; Gerbera/Rygel for servers), on the DTCP-IP/DTLA DRM blocker being the key obstacle for protected content, and on the DLNA org dissolution/SpireSpark transition. Medium on the precise push-vs-pull and DMR-vs-DMP terminology mapping (commonly confused — flagged), and on the exact DLNA guideline version details (media-profile counts, when DTCP-IP is conditionally mandatory) since the DLNA guidelines themselves are paywalled and I relied on secondary/reconstructed sources for those specifics.

name: Wireless CarPlay
category: automotive-projection (phone-to-head-unit screen/app projection); built on AirPlay screen-mirroring + iAP2 accessory protocol
summary: Wireless CarPlay is Apple's protocol for projecting a car-optimized iPhone UI onto a vehicle head unit (the receiver/"sink"). It is not a generic mirror of the phone screen; the iPhone renders a dedicated CarPlay UI and streams it as H.264 video plus audio to the head unit, while touch/knob input and metadata flow back. Technically it is Apple's AirPlay screen-mirroring stack wrapped in the iAP2/MFi accessory framework: Bluetooth bootstraps the pairing and hands off Wi-Fi credentials, then the AirPlay session runs over Wi-Fi. Building an open receiver is gated primarily by Apple's MFi licensing program and its hardware authentication coprocessor, not by protocol secrecy alone.
transmitterPlatforms: iPhone (iOS) is the sole first-party transmitter/source. There is no public transmitter SDK; the iOS CarPlay framework only lets third-party APPS render into an Apple-controlled CarPlay UI, not implement the wire protocol.

Reverse-engineered/clone transmitters exist: dongles and Android projects (okcar-os/autoconn) emulate an iPhone-side to feed a head unit, but these are unauthorized and often rely on cloned MFi behavior.
receiverPlatforms: OEM/aftermarket car head units (the intended receiver), which must be MFi-CarPlay certified and contain an Apple Authentication Coprocessor.
Carlinkit / CPlay2Air / 'Autobox' USB dongles (i.MX6UL Linux devices) that act as a licensed CarPlay receiver and re-expose the decoded stream over USB.

Raspberry Pi / Linux / Android via open-source host software (react-carplay/node-carplay, pycarplay, FastCarPlay, carplay-receiver) — but these DRIVE a Carlinkit dongle; the dongle, not the open code, is the actual CarPlay receiver.
Android natively via okcar-os (reverse-engineered, no dongle) — the rare project claiming a native RE receiver, built from purchased packet captures.
howItWorks: Discovery/bootstrap: the head unit advertises over Bluetooth; the iPhone connects via iAP2 over Bluetooth RFCOMM (SDP UUID 00000000-deca-fade-deca-deafdecacaff for accessories). iAP2 runs MFi accessory identification and authentication, then the phone issues an iAP2 message to request the accessory's Wi-Fi configuration (RequestAccessoryWiFiConfigurationInformation, control 0x5702) to obtain SSID + password. Handoff: the iPhone joins the head unit's Wi-Fi (the head unit runs a soft-AP / private Wi-Fi network). Over Wi-Fi it discovers AirPlay services via Bonjour/mDNS. Session: an AirPlay session is established and secured by an internal HomeKit-style pairing (pair-setup/pair-verify handshake). The iPhone then renders the dedicated CarPlay UI, encodes it as H.264 video (up to ~60fps/1080p on capable links) with audio, and streams it to the head unit; touch/rotary/button input and now-playing metadata are returned. iAP2 continues to tunnel control/accessory data alongside the AirPlay media. Wired CarPlay is the same AirPlay session but tunneled over a USB NCM virtual-ethernet endpoint instead of Wi-Fi, with Bluetooth not needed for bootstrap.
lowerLevelProtocols: Bluetooth Classic (RFCOMM/SDP) for iAP2 bootstrap and Wi-Fi credential exchange
Wi-Fi (head unit soft-AP; 2.4/5 GHz) as the media transport
iAP2 (iPod Accessory Protocol 2) — Apple's framed accessory/session protocol (magic 0xFF 0x5A)
Bonjour / mDNS (DNS-SD) for AirPlay service discovery
AirPlay (screen-mirroring variant) over RTSP/HTTP-style setup + RTP-like media streaming
HomeKit-style pairing handshake (SRP-based pair-setup, Curve25519/Ed25519 pair-verify) securing the AirPlay session

authEncryption: Two layered auth systems. (1) MFi hardware authentication: the accessory (head unit or dongle) must contain an Apple Authentication Coprocessor chip. The iPhone requests the chip's Apple-signed certificate, sends a challenge, and the chip signs it (documented as RSA-1024/SHA-1 in older iAP; MFi-SAP derives AES-128-CTR session keys). This proves genuine MFi hardware and is the core DRM/gating mechanism — the private key is inside Apple-supplied silicon and cannot be extracted or software-emulated legitimately. (2) AirPlay/HomeKit session security: pair-setup (SRP) and pair-verify (Curve25519/Ed25519) establish an encrypted session for the mirrored video/audio and control channel. Note a commonly-cited asymmetry: iAP2 authentication is largely one-way — the phone authenticates the head unit, but the head unit does not strongly authenticate the phone, which underpins several attack/impersonation writeups. Clone dongles use counterfeit auth chips or replay expected iAP2 sequences to pass the challenge without genuine Apple silicon.
