protocolDocs: Mixed. The official CarPlay/MFi specification is licensed-under-NDA only (available to MFi-CarPlay members). Apple publishes high-level security notes (Apple Platform Security guide: accessory verification, MFi-SAP, AES-128-CTR). The heavy lifting for outsiders is reverse-engineered: strong writeups include wiomoc.de's iAP/iAP2 analysis, the Oligo Security 'Pwn My Ride' CarPlay attack-surface post (CVE-2025-24132), a USENIX VehicleSec'25 paper on third-party CarPlay adapter security, TROOPERS24 'Apple CarPlay: What's Under the Hood' (Nöttgen), an OhioLink MS thesis on the 'Magic Box' screen adapter, and the ludwig-v dongle RE repo. The AirPlay/HomeKit-pairing layers are well-documented by the OpenAirPlay/UxPlay community. No official public byte-level CarPlay spec exists.
receiverFeasibility: Building an open receiver splits into two very different problems. Protocol-wise it is largely tractable: the transport (Bluetooth iAP2 bootstrap -> Wi-Fi handoff -> Bonjour discovery -> AirPlay mirroring session over HomeKit pairing -> H.264 decode) is reasonably understood from RE work and overlaps heavily with existing open AirPlay-mirroring receivers. The hard blocker is authentication/DRM: the iPhone requires proof of a genuine Apple Authentication Coprocessor during iAP2/MFi-SAP. That private key lives in Apple-controlled silicon with no legitimate software emulation, and the chip is sold only to audited MFi licensees. So a fully open, chip-free, sanctioned receiver is effectively impossible without Apple. The pragmatic open path everyone actually uses is to buy a licensed Carlinkit/Autobox dongle (which owns the auth) and write open host software that drives it over USB — react-carplay, pycarplay, FastCarPlay. A native no-dongle receiver (okcar-os) requires either a genuine harvested auth chip or a legally/ethically dubious clone/bypass. Practical scope for an open project: dongle-driven USB host + H.264 decode + input mapping + CANbus glue is a weekend-to-months effort; a native standalone receiver is a licensing wall, not just an engineering one.
transmitterNotes: The iPhone transmitter is closed and non-substitutable for legitimate use; iOS exposes only a CarPlay app framework (render into Apple's UI), never the wire protocol. Emulating the transmitter (to feed a head unit from non-Apple hardware) is what okcar-os/autoconn and some Android head-unit hacks attempt, and it also runs into the MFi challenge (the head unit expects to authenticate against, and be authenticated by, genuine Apple behavior). Note the frequently-cited one-way-auth asymmetry makes phone-impersonation attacks on head units easier than the reverse. Transmitter-side open work is much rarer and legally shakier than the dongle-driven receiver ecosystem.

contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Directionally true (it rides the AirPlay mirroring stack + HomeKit pairing) but oversimplified: CarPlay adds the iAP2/MFi accessory layer, a dedicated CarPlay UI rendered on the phone (not a raw phone-screen mirror), and bidirectional input/metadata. Plain AirPlay receivers cannot accept a CarPlay session.

contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Commonly misreported. They are HOST software that drives a licensed Carlinkit/Autobox dongle over USB; the dongle contains the actual CarPlay/AirPlay/MFi receiver and the auth chip. The open code decodes video and handles I/O, not the protocol/auth.

contestedClaims.whyUncertain: OpenAuto and Crankshaft are Android AUTO head-unit emulators (aasdk-based) and never implemented CarPlay. OpenAuto Pro adds CarPlay only by integrating a Carlinkit CPC200-Autokit dongle. Frequently conflated.

contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Sourced from RE writeups and older iAP documentation; newer coprocessor generations (e.g., the 3.0 auth IC) and CarPlay revisions may use different/updated primitives. Byte-level specifics are not officially published and may vary by generation.

contestedClaims.whyUncertain: The royalty figure is rumor-level, not an official Apple number. And the barrier is BOTH: the full CarPlay spec is NDA-gated AND the auth chip is required — characterizing it as chip-only understates the licensing/spec wall.

contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Reported by the Oligo/CarPlay security research and underpins impersonation CVEs, but the exact mutual-auth behavior may differ across wired vs wireless and across CarPlay versions; treat as security-research finding rather than settled spec.

contestedClaims.whyUncertain: It claims native RE implementation but the author states core protocol/captures were purchased from third parties; completeness, legality (MFi bypass), and how it satisfies the auth challenge are unverified.

confidence: Medium-high on architecture (AirPlay + iAP2 + Bluetooth/Wi-Fi bootstrap + MFi auth chip gating) and on the open/closed implementation landscape, all cross-checked across RE writeups, security papers, and project repos. Lower confidence on exact cryptographic primitives/key sizes, per-device royalty figures, and the precise mutual-auth semantics, which are RE/rumor-sourced and version-dependent.

name: Wireless Android Auto (Android Auto Projection Protocol / AAP)
category: screen-mirroring / phone-projection (with app-launch + input backchannel); rides USB (AOAP) or Wi-Fi transport
summary: Android Auto projection is a phone-to-head-unit protocol in which the phone renders a car-optimized UI and streams it as H.264 video (plus audio) to the head unit, while the head unit sends touch/rotary/button input, microphone audio, and vehicle sensor data back. It is a protobuf-over-TLS, multiplexed multi-channel protocol carried either over USB using the Android Open Accessory Protocol (AOAP) or wirelessly over a Wi-Fi link that is bootstrapped by a short Bluetooth handshake. It is distinct from Android Automotive OS (an embedded in-car OS, not projection). A substantial reverse-engineered open ecosystem exists (aasdk/openauto and successors) because Google publishes no public spec, and unlike Apple CarPlay there is no mandatory hardware authentication chip on the head-unit side, which makes an open receiver comparatively feasible.
transmitterPlatforms: Android phone running the Android Auto app (Android 8+/9+ for wireless; the source of the projected UI)
The phone is the projection SOURCE: it decodes app content and encodes it to H.264, and in the wireless case it acts as the TLS/TCP client that dials the head unit
No third-party transmitter SDK: only Google's Android Auto app produces the protocol; app developers target the Android for Cars App Library / templates, not the wire protocol
receiverPlatforms: Certified car head units (OEM and aftermarket, e.g. Pioneer/Kenwood/Sony/Alpine) — the intended sink
Google's own x86_64 'headunit' desktop emulator/reference receiver binary (statically linked OpenH264, PortAudio, OpenSSL)
Reverse-engineered open receivers: openauto/aasdk on Raspberry Pi (Crankshaft, openDsh/dash), headunit-revived/headunit, LIVI (Linux/macOS/Windows Electron head unit)
Wireless dongles that act as a USB head-unit to the phone and re-emit over Wi-Fi (WirelessAndroidAutoDongle/aawgd, aa-proxy-rs) — technically a receiver+bridge
howItWorks: DISCOVERY/TRANSPORT: Over USB, the head unit uses AOAP (Android Open Accessory) vendor requests to switch the phone into accessory mode, then bulk endpoints carry the stream. Wirelessly, the head unit advertises a Bluetooth device and RFCOMM service; the phone connects over BT and the two exchange a small set of protobuf messages (notably WifiStartRequest carrying the head unit's TCP IP/port — commonly 10.0.0.1:5288 — and WifiInfoRequest/WifiInfoResponse carrying Wi-Fi SSID/BSSID/credentials). The phone then joins the Wi-Fi network (head-unit-hosted AP or Wi-Fi Direct group) and opens a TCP socket; Bluetooth's job is essentially done (it may stay for HFP hands-free calling). SESSION: Regardless of transport, the two sides speak the same framed protocol: a control channel first does a version handshake, then a TLS handshake is performed inside the protocol (the head unit initiates the SSL handshake after the version response; the phone/AA app will not proceed without a valid TLS context). After auth-complete, the head unit sends a ServiceDiscoveryRequest and the phone replies with a ServiceDiscoveryResponse enumerating services. CHANNELS: The link is multiplexed into channels/services — control, video (H.264 sink), media/system/speech audio (sink), microphone audio (source), input/touch, sensor (vehicle data source), bluetooth, plus AV setup/media-status. Each frame carries a channel id, flags (including an encrypted bit), and length; payloads are protobuf messages, and most traffic after the handshake is TLS-encrypted. The head unit opens the video channel, negotiates resolution/DPI/framerate, and continuously receives an H.264 elementary stream to decode, while feeding input and sensor messages upstream.
lowerLevelProtocols: USB Android Open Accessory Protocol (AOAP / AOA 2.0) with bulk endpoints (wired transport)
Bluetooth RFCOMM + a head-unit BT profile, plus HFP (Hands-Free Profile) for calls (wireless bootstrap)
Wi-Fi: head-unit-hosted AP or Wi-Fi Direct, typically 5 GHz
TCP (default port ~5288) as the wireless session socket
TLS (via OpenSSL) as the in-protocol encryption layer
Protocol Buffers for structured messages
H.264 (AVC) for video; PCM/audio channels for audio
authEncryption: Authentication is a TLS handshake performed inside the AAP control channel (OpenSSL). The head unit initiates the SSL handshake right after protocol version negotiation, and the Android Auto app refuses to continue without it. It is a certificate-based TLS exchange (effectively mutual TLS with head-unit and mobile-device certs; open MITM tools use hu_key/hu_cert.pem and md_key/md_cert.pem). Crucially — and this is the key contrast with CarPlay — there is NO mandatory dedicated hardware authentication coprocessor on the head-unit side. This is why open-source receivers can complete the handshake using certificates recovered from Google's own reference receiver/emulator. Wireless credentials (Wi-Fi SSID/PSK) are passed over the Bluetooth bootstrap in protobuf messages. Note that content DRM (e.g. Widevine for protected media) is a separate, app/content-level concern layered on top and is not the projection-link auth.

protocolDocs: No official public specification. The wire protocol is reverse-engineered only. Key open documentation: milek7's Android Auto protocol research notes (galdocs), the aasdk/openauto source and their extracted .proto files (common.proto, protos.proto), the XDA 'Reverse engineering AA USB protocol' thread (headunit lineage), and the WirelessAndroidAutoDongle/aa-proxy-rs code+issues for the wireless BT bootstrap. Google publishes app-developer docs (Android for Cars App Library) and head-unit certification/compliance material, but nothing describing the framing, channels, or handshake at the wire level.
receiverFeasibility: Comparatively feasible and already done in the open — this is the strong part of the story. Because there is no mandatory head-unit-side hardware auth chip (contrast CarPlay's MFi coprocessor), an open receiver can complete the in-protocol TLS handshake using certificates recovered from Google's reference receiver, and mature open stacks (aasdk/openauto, LIVI, headunit) prove end-to-end operation. What a builder needs: (1) transport — USB gadget/AOAP handling, or the Bluetooth+Wi-Fi bootstrap for wireless; (2) the protobuf schemas and frame multiplexer with the TLS layer; (3) an H.264 decoder and audio sink, plus input/sensor sources. Real blockers are practical rather than cryptographic: reliance on RE'd protobuf definitions and possibly-non-redistributable reference certificates, no spec so behavior tracks Google app changes and can break, GPLv3 licensing on the core libraries, and the fact that you cannot legally ship a CERTIFIED/logo'd product without Google's head-unit certification even though the tech works. DRM only matters for specific protected media content, not for bringing the link up.
transmitterNotes: The transmitter side is essentially closed: only Google's Android Auto app emits the protocol, there is no public transmitter SDK, and the phone holds the encoder and TLS keys. Building an open transmitter (pretending to be a phone to drive a real car head unit) is far rarer than building receivers, but has been demonstrated (e.g. tomasz-grobelny/AACS, and the phone-facing side of dongle projects). For most systems engineers the interesting/tractable target is the receiver. Wireless dongles are hybrid: they present a wireless-head-unit face to the phone (transmitter-facing) and a wired-head-unit face to the car, so they exercise both sides of the bootstrap.

contestedClaims.claim: The in-protocol TLS is full mutual TLS and uses a single shared/hardcoded certificate that any head unit can reuse (as opposed to per-device provisioned certs).
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Open receivers clearly work using certs recovered from Google's reference receiver, implying a shared/reusable credential and no per-unit hardware root of trust — but I could not directly confirm whether it is strictly a single hardcoded cert, whether client-auth is enforced in both directions, or whether newer AA versions tightened this. name: Samsung Smart View / Quick Share / Tap View (Samsung casting & sharing stack)
category: Umbrella brand covering multiple distinct mechanisms: screen-mirroring (Miracast-based), media/app-launch casting (DIAL + MSF WebSocket), proximity-triggered handoff (Tap View), and peer file-transfer (Quick Share). Mix of standard substrates with Samsung/Google proprietary discovery and control layers.
summary: "Samsung Smart View / Quick Share / Tap View" is not one protocol but a family of features Samsung markets under friendly names, each layering proprietary discovery/control on top of industry standards. Smart View (the phone-to-TV screen-mirroring toggle) rides on Wi-Fi Direct + Miracast (WFD) for the actual pixels, while media/app casting to Samsung TVs uses DIAL/SSDP discovery plus Samsung's proprietary MSF WebSocket "MultiScreen" control channel. Tap View is a UX trigger (bump-detection via accelerometer + BLE proximity, orchestrated by SmartThings) that then launches an ordinary Smart View mirroring session. Quick Share is a peer file-transfer system (BLE discovery + Wi-Fi Direct/Aware transport) that, as of 2024, has been merged with Google's Nearby Share into a single unified "Quick Share" protocol distributed through Google Play Services.
transmitterPlatforms: Samsung Galaxy phones/tablets: Smart View mirroring toggle in the quick panel (native in One UI); Quick Share native; Tap View trigger via SmartThings app
Generic Android: Miracast (WFD) mirroring where OEM keeps it; unified Quick Share via Google Play Services (Nearby Share successor)
Windows: Samsung Quick Share app (Galaxy Book, Microsoft Store) and Google's Quick Share for Windows app for non-Samsung PCs; Miracast 'Connect'/'Cast' built into Windows
ChromeOS: unified Quick Share (91+)
iOS/macOS: no native Samsung mirroring transmitter; interop via AirPlay 2 (separate Apple stack Samsung TVs receive) and, since late 2025, Quick Share<->AirDrop file interop
App developers: Smart View SDK (Android/iOS/JS senders) for casting/launching Tizen receiver apps
receiverPlatforms: Samsung Smart TVs (Tizen, ~2016+) and some Orsay-era H/J-series (2014-15): act as Miracast sink ('Screen Mirroring' source), DIAL/MSF app-launch target, Tap View mirroring sink, and AirPlay 2 receiver
Samsung smart monitors and some Family Hub appliances: Smart View / SmartThings casting targets
Generic Miracast sinks (any WFD-certified display/dongle/Windows PC in 'Connect' mode): can receive the Smart View mirror because that layer is standard Miracast
Quick Share receivers: Galaxy phones, any Android via Google Play Services, Windows (both apps), ChromeOS; unofficially macOS/Linux via reverse-engineered clients
howItWorks: Four separable flows. (1) Screen mirroring (Smart View toggle -> Samsung TV 'Screen Mirroring'): device discovery via BLE/SmartThings and Wi-Fi Direct service discovery; the media plane is Miracast/Wi-Fi Display (WFD) — an ad-hoc Wi-Fi Direct link carrying H.264 over RTP/RTSP, with HDCP 2.x on protected content. To a generic Miracast sink this looks like standard Miracast. (2) Media/app casting: Samsung TVs advertise via SSDP/DIAL (UPnP) and mDNS; senders discover them and use Samsung's proprietary MSF 'MultiScreen' WebSocket channel (ws on :8001, wss on :8002, endpoints under /api/v2/ e.g. samsung.remote.control and application channels) to launch/communicate with Tizen HTML5 receiver apps and drive the TV remote. This is where Samsung diverges most from Google Cast. (3) Tap View: SmartThings must be enabled; bringing the phone near/against the TV is detected by the phone's accelerometer (a 'bump') combined with BLE proximity, prompting a presence-detection allow dialog; on accept it simply auto-starts a normal Smart View/Miracast mirroring session — the tap is only the trigger, not a transport. (4) Quick Share: BLE advertisement/handshake for discovery+auth, then a direct Wi-Fi link (Wi-Fi Direct/Aware, or same-LAN mDNS in the unified version) for bulk transfer; Bluetooth or Samsung Cloud/link fallback for distant or blocked cases. Since 2024 the discovery/transfer protocol is Google's Nearby Share design (mDNS + ECDSA key exchange, AES + HMAC-SHA256 secured sessions).
lowerLevelProtocols: Wi-Fi Direct (P2P) — substrate for Miracast mirroring and Quick Share transfer
Miracast / Wi-Fi Display (WFD) — Wi-Fi Alliance mirroring standard: RTSP control, RTP media, H.264 (mandatory), optional H.265, LPCM/AAC audio, WPA2 link
HDCP 2.x — link content protection over the Miracast session
SSDP / UPnP / DIAL — TV discovery and app-launch for casting
mDNS/DNS-SD — device discovery (casting; unified Quick Share transfer)
WebSocket / HTTP(S) — Samsung MSF MultiScreen control channel and REST/WS remote API
BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy) — Quick Share discovery/handshake, Tap View proximity, SmartThings signaling
TLS/WSS — encrypted variant of the TV control channel (:8002)
Bluetooth Classic — Quick Share slow-path fallback
Wi-Fi Aware (NAN) — optional discovery/transport for Quick Share on supported hardware
authEncryption: Distinct per flow. Miracast mirroring: standard WFD pairing over WPA2 Wi-Fi Direct with optional PIN; HDCP 2.x may be negotiated for protected content, which is the main DRM blocker for a full open sink. MSF TV control (:8001/:8002): first connection triggers an on-TV allow/permission prompt; the TV issues a token that the client stores and replays (query param/handshake); :8002 wraps it in TLS. Tap View: gated by an explicit on-phone 'allow phone presence detection' consent; the mirror itself is then normal Miracast auth. Quick Share (unified): BLE-advertised presence with visibility scoping (everyone / contacts-only / your-devices / off); session security uses ECDSA key exchange with AES-CBC + HMAC-SHA256 (Google Nearby Share crypto); Samsung-account or Google-account sign-in is used for contacts/'your devices' targeting and for Samsung Cloud fallback, but not strictly required for 'everyone'-mode transfers. Quick Share<->AirDrop interop (2025+) works only in 'Everyone for 10 minutes' mode.

protocolDocs: Mixed. (1) Miracast/WFD: official spec exists but is behind Wi-Fi Alliance membership; well understood publicly and reimplemented (MiracleCast). (2) Samsung MSF/Smart View SDK: officially documented at developer.samsung.com and via the SmartViewSDK GitHub API guide, but the low-level MSF WebSocket wire protocol is primarily known via reverse engineering (xchwarze/samsung-tv-ws-api, plus xchwarze's COMMANDS.md). DIAL itself is a published spec (Netflix/YouTube, co-developed with Sony/Samsung); DIALStranger documents its security weaknesses. (3) Quick Share/Nearby Share: no official protocol spec; the authoritative public description is grishka/NearDrop's reverse-engineered PROTOCOL.md, corroborated by rquickshare. (4) Tap View: no protocol spec — only Samsung support/UX docs; the accelerometer-bump + BLE mechanism is inferred, not documented. (5) Quick Share<->AirDrop interop is described in Google's Nov-2025 security blog.
receiverFeasibility: Feasibility splits sharply by flow. MIRRORING SINK (most-requested 'receive Smart View'): tractable, because Smart View mirroring is essentially standard Miracast/WFD — MiracleCast already implements a Linux sink. Blockers are (a) Wi-Fi Direct P2P support and driver quirks, (b) HDCP 2.x — you can receive unprotected screens but cannot decrypt HDCP-protected content without licensed keys, and (c) some Samsung-specific discovery niceties (SmartThings/BLE handshakes, Tap View) that you would skip in favor of plain Miracast connect. CASTING/CONTROL RECEIVER (pretend to be a Samsung TV for DIAL+MSF): the control plane is reverse-engineered and reimplementable (WebSocket server + DIAL/SSDP advertisement + Tizen-style app model), but sender apps expect Tizen HTML5 receiver semantics, so a faithful open receiver is high-effort and low-payoff. QUICK SHARE SINK: very tractable and already done unofficially (NearDrop/rquickshare/packet) — you need mDNS, ECDSA key exchange, AES-CBC + HMAC-SHA256; the main friction is that BLE/Wi-Fi-Direct discovery paths are less documented than the Wi-Fi-LAN path, and 'contacts'/'your devices' modes need account attestation you cannot forge. TAP VIEW SINK: not independently buildable in practice — it depends on Samsung TV firmware presence-detection and SmartThings orchestration; an open receiver would just fall back to being a Miracast sink and lose the tap trigger. Net: build a Miracast sink for mirroring and a Nearby/Quick Share client for files; treat the MSF casting receiver and Tap View as impractical/closed.
transmitterNotes: Transmitter side is easier across the board. Mirroring: any Miracast/WFD source (Windows 'Connect', MiracleCast, GNOME Network Displays, most non-Samsung Androids) can drive a Samsung TV's 'Screen Mirroring' sink since that layer is standard. TV control/app-launch: fully practical today via reverse-engineered MSF WebSocket libraries (samsung-tv-ws-api, HA integrations) for remote keys, app launch, Frame Art Mode, browser — but these do not stream media, they control. Media casting to a Tizen receiver app requires Samsung's Smart View SDK sender model. Quick Share: sending is straightforward from any device with the unified client; open Rust/Swift clients can transmit as well. Note the deprecations/renames: the standalone 'Smart View' remote app was killed Oct 2020 (folded into SmartThings); 'Smart View' now names only the mirroring toggle. Google ended support for Samsung's own Galaxy Book Quick Share Windows app (May 2025) in favor of Google's Windows app.

contestedClaims.whyUncertain: The media plane is Miracast (H.264/RTP over Wi-Fi Direct) and generic Miracast sinks do receive it, but Samsung wraps discovery/session setup with proprietary SmartThings/BLE signaling; Google removed native Miracast from Android 6.0, so Samsung's OEM implementation may diverge in discovery/negotiation even though the stream is standard. name: Xiaomi / Huawei / Android OEM Casting (Miracast + proprietary extensions)
aka: Huawei Cast+ / Cast Engine / Cast Kit
category: screen-mirroring (with adjacent media-URL-casting via DLNA and app-handoff via vendor multi-screen collaboration)
summary: Android OEM phone-to-display casting is a layered story: a common industry baseline (Wi-Fi Alliance Miracast, i.e. "HDMI over Wi-Fi Direct") plus per-vendor proprietary extensions that mostly replace or wrap it. Xiaomi's "Screen Cast/Cast" in MIUI/HyperOS is largely standards-based Miracast for mirroring plus DLNA/UPnP for media-URL casting, with lightly proprietary phone-to-phone/tablet variants. Huawei Cast+ (exposed to developers as Cast Engine / Cast Kit) is a genuinely proprietary alternative to Miracast: it runs its own streaming/transport protocol tuned for lossy Wi-Fi (claims ~25% packet-loss tolerance) and, per Huawei's own docs, is NOT interoperable with Miracast/AirPlay/Google Cast on non-Huawei devices — though Huawei devices generally also speak Miracast and DLNA as fallbacks. HONOR (formerly Huawei) inherits much of the same stack; OPPO/vivo/realme lean on Miracast + DLNA plus proprietary PC/tablet "multi-screen collaboration" suites.

howItWorks: Two distinct casting shapes are commonly conflated. (1) Screen MIRRORING: the phone encodes its framebuffer live and streams it. The Miracast baseline discovers peers over Wi-Fi Direct (P2P) using WPS/WPA2 to form an ad-hoc link (or over existing Wi-Fi infrastructure via MS-MICE), then negotiates codecs and controls the session with an RTSP dialect (WFD), carrying H.264 (optionally HEVC) video + LPCM/AAC audio in MPEG2-TS over RTP/UDP. (2) MEDIA-URL CASTING: apps hand a content URL to a DLNA/UPnP renderer discovered via SSDP; the TV fetches and plays it (this is 'casting' proper, closer to Google Cast, and needs no continuous encode). Vendor proprietary layers change (1): Huawei Cast+ replaces the Wi-Fi-Direct+RTSP+RTP stack with its own discovery (typically mDNS/SSDP-style on the LAN or P2P) and a custom streaming/transport protocol with FEC/anti-jitter tuned for lossy channels, plus 'resource/stream projection' where only a media handle is sent so the sink renders natively (lower latency, higher quality than raw mirroring). Cast Engine also enables 'app projection' / multi-screen collaboration (phone app UI mirrored/controlled on a large screen). OPPO/vivo/HONOR PC-connect suites layer file transfer, reverse control, and clipboard over their own transports on top of, or instead of, Miracast.
lowerLevelProtocols: Wi-Fi Direct (P2P) with WPS/WPA2 — Miracast link setup
IEEE 802.11 infrastructure Wi-Fi (Miracast over Infrastructure / MS-MICE; and all DLNA/Cast+ LAN modes)
RTSP (WFD dialect) — Miracast session control
RTP/UDP over IP + MPEG2-TS container — Miracast media transport
H.264/AVC (mandatory), H.265/HEVC (optional) video; LPCM (mandatory), AAC/AC3/E-AC3 audio
mDNS/DNS-SD and SSDP/UPnP — discovery for DLNA and vendor (Cast+) modes
DLNA/UPnP AV (SSDP + SOAP + HTTP) — media-URL casting path
HDCP 2.x — link content protection (Miracast)
TDLS/optional; proprietary FEC-based transport for Huawei Cast+ (details not public)
authEncryption: Miracast baseline: the underlying Wi-Fi Direct link is set up via WPS and secured with WPA2, so the transport is encrypted at the link layer; there is no separate application-level device pairing beyond a PIN/PBC in some flows. Content protection is HDCP 2.x negotiated over the WFD/RTSP session — but it is applied per-content: unprotected content streams without HDCP, while premium/DRM'd content (e.g. certain video apps) will require the sink to present a valid HDCP 2.2 receiver certificate or the source blacks out or refuses that content. So an open sink can mirror general UI/most content but will fail on HDCP-gated streams because it cannot obtain a licensed HDCP key/certificate. DLNA path: typically no encryption and no strong auth (LAN trust), though DRM'd media won't be served. Huawei Cast+ / Cast Engine: proprietary. Uses its own discovery and (per Huawei) is delivered to sink manufacturers as signed binary packages under a UX/certification spec, implying vendor-controlled authentication/keys; exact pairing/encryption scheme is not publicly documented. Vendor multi-screen suites often add account-based trust (same Huawei/Xiaomi/OPPO ID auto-connects nearby devices).

protocolDocs: Mixed. Miracast: the Wi-Fi Alliance now publishes the Miracast Specification (v2.3 seen at wi-fi.org) and technical overviews/tech notes publicly, and it builds on public IETF RTSP/RTP and Wi-Fi Direct specs — so the mirroring baseline is well-documented, plus Intel's open wds/libwds and MiracleCast serve as executable references. HDCP adaptation for Miracast is documented but the keys/certs are licensed (Digital CP). Huawei Cast+/Cast Engine: essentially no public protocol spec — Huawei's developer pages describe capabilities and integration requirements (UX spec, binary delivery) but not the wire protocol; understanding is limited to marketing/patent filings (multiple USPTO 'screen projection method' patents) and inference, so it is effectively reverse-engineered-only/none for an outside implementer. OPPO/vivo/HONOR collaboration transports: none public.
receiverFeasibility: For a Miracast sink (covers Xiaomi mirroring and the fallback mode of Huawei/HONOR/OPPO/vivo phones): FEASIBLE and already done — MiracleCast + wpa_supplicant (Wi-Fi Direct/WFD) + GStreamer is the proven open stack. Main blockers are (a) Wi-Fi hardware/driver P2P support quality, and (b) HDCP: you cannot license/provision HDCP receiver keys as an open project, so any HDCP-gated content (some streaming apps, protected video) will refuse to display — general UI/screen mirroring still works. Supporting the DLNA media-URL path (what MIUI/EMUI media apps often use) is EASIER still, with mature open UPnP renderers and no HDCP for served content. For a Huawei Cast+ sink specifically: HARD/impractical today — proprietary undocumented transport, no open implementation, vendor-signed binary integration and (implied) key-based device authentication; you'd be reverse-engineering from scratch with no reference. Pragmatic strategy for an open receiver: implement Miracast sink + DLNA renderer to catch the standards-based modes of all these OEMs, and accept that Cast+/AirPlay-class proprietary modes are out of reach without vendor keys.
transmitterNotes: Transmitter is generally harder to do openly than the sink for the mirroring path: AOSP dropped the public Miracast/Wi-Fi Display source API at Android 6.0, and OEMs re-implement it privately in their frameworks, so there is no supported app-level way to originate a raw Miracast stream from a stock Android app — you either use the OEM system UI (Cast/Wireless Projection), a vendor SDK, or DLNA/UPnP as a controller. MiracleCast's source side is incomplete, so open Miracast transmit is weak. The practical open transmitter path from a phone is DLNA/UPnP (push a media URL) or Google Cast (separate ecosystem), not Miracast. Huawei Cast+ transmit is only available through Huawei devices/Cast Kit SDK. For a systems engineer, the realistic sender you control is either the phone's built-in OEM caster (interop-test against your open sink) or a DLNA controller you write.

name: Spotify Connect
category: app-specific-handoff (proprietary control-plane + cloud-mediated playback handoff); not screen-mirroring and not media-URL casting
summary: Spotify Connect is Spotify's proprietary system for controlling playback across devices and handing playback off between them. Crucially, the receiver device streams the audio itself directly from Spotify's cloud/CDN — the phone or PC acts only as a remote control, not as a media relay (unlike Bluetooth/AirPlay audio, and unlike Chromecast media-URL casting where a generic URL is handed over). The controller and receiver coordinate largely via Spotify's cloud (a "dealer" WebSocket push channel), with an additional local mDNS/zeroconf path used mainly to log a Spotify account into a nearby hardware device without typing a password. The protocol is closed; open receivers exist only via reverse engineering (librespot family), and a licensed C-API "eSDK" exists for approved hardware makers.

howItWorks: Two coupled planes. (1) Control/session plane: a device authenticates to a Spotify Access Point (AP) over a Shannon-encrypted TCP connection, then maintains a persistent 'dealer' WebSocket to the cloud that carries remote-control commands and playback-state sync. Devices advertise their presence and state to Spotify's backend, so a controller can list and target any of the user's logged-in devices regardless of network. Selecting a device or 'transferring playback' sends a command through the cloud; the receiver then independently fetches metadata (SpClient REST) and pulls the actual audio from Spotify's CDN via HTTPS range requests and plays it locally. The phone is not in the audio path. (2) Local zeroconf onboarding plane: a hardware receiver advertises _spotify-connect._tcp via mDNS/DNS-SD (Bonjour-compatible) and runs a small HTTP server exposing getInfo and addUser. A nearby, already-authenticated Spotify app discovers it, does a Diffie-Hellman exchange, and POSTs the user's identity plus an encrypted credential 'blob' to addUser so the device can log into the user's account without a typed password. After that, the device appears as a normal cloud-visible Connect target.

AES-128-CTR (audio content decryption)
authEncryption: Account auth is token/blob-based, never sharing the raw password with the device. AP session: client sends ClientResponseEncrypted (packet 0xab) with LoginCredentials; AP replies APWelcome (0xac) or APLoginFailed (0xad). After the plaintext handshake, all packets use a Shannon cipher with a 4-byte big-endian nonce incremented per packet, with separate send/recv keys. Historically login could be username+password (AUTHENTICATION_USER_PASS); modern flows use stored reusable credentials or OAuth-derived tokens, and access tokens for APIs are minted via the 'keymaster' endpoint (hm://keymaster/). Zeroconf onboarding: DH shared secret -> base_key=SHA1(shared_secret); encryption_key=HMAC-SHA1(base_key,\"encryption\")[:16], checksum_key=HMAC-SHA1(base_key,\"checksum\"); blob = AES128-CTR-DECRYPT(encryption_key, IV, ciphertext) with an HMAC-SHA1 MAC check. The inner reusable blob is further unwrapped with base_key = PBKDF2(SHA1(deviceID), username, 0x100 iters), then AES-192 decrypt to recover login_data. Content protection: audio files are AES-128-CTR encrypted; historically the per-track key was fetched over the AP with a fixed AUDIO_AESIV, but Spotify has migrated to a 'PlayPlay' DRM scheme that obfuscates the returned key with a hardcoded client-side key, plus Widevine/FairPlay paths for some tiers (notably higher-bitrate/lossless).

protocolDocs: Mixed. The local zeroconf onboarding surface is the ONLY officially-documented piece — Spotify publishes a public ZeroConf API guide under its Commercial Hardware docs (getInfo/addUser, service type, TXT CPath, required fields). The eSDK API reference is public in outline but the implementation is a licensed binary under NDA. Everything else — AP handshake, Shannon cipher, dealer WebSocket, audio key retrieval, PlayPlay DRM — is documented only via reverse-engineering writeups: librespot's docs/authentication.md and docs/connection.md, the librespot wiki, librespot-org/spotify-connect-resources data dumps, and GitHub discussions (e.g. librespot-java #421 on PlayPlay). Some reverse-eng repos have been hit by DMCA takedowns.
receiverFeasibility: Building an open receiver is well-trodden but fragile. The mechanics are proven: zeroconf onboarding is officially documented and the AP/session/audio path is fully reverse-engineered in librespot, so a systems engineer can stand up a working Connect sink on embedded Linux quickly by embedding/porting librespot or go-librespot rather than reimplementing from scratch. The real blockers are: (1) Premium account requirement — free-tier Connect requires the licensed eSDK, so open receivers effectively need Premium credentials; (2) content DRM drift — audio is AES-128-CTR but the key-provisioning has moved to the 'PlayPlay' scheme that obfuscates keys with a hardcoded client key not publicly cracked, plus Widevine/FairPlay for higher/lossless tiers, so lossless is explicitly not supported by open clients; (3) ongoing protocol churn — Spotify periodically changes login/token flows (keymaster 403s, OAuth requirements) that break clients until re-reversed; (4) legal exposure — no license, ToS violation, and DMCA takedowns of some tooling. There is NO hardware auth chip requirement (unlike AirPlay's historical MFi coprocessor), so the barrier is software/DRM and legal, not silicon.
transmitterNotes: Transmitter (controller) side is easier in shape than the receiver: it means discovering the user's devices (via cloud + optional local zeroconf), authenticating to Spotify, and issuing transfer/play/pause/volume commands over the dealer WebSocket / Connect state API. librespot-java and go-librespot can act as controllers, and there are thin scripts (e.g. spotify-zeroconf) that just do the local addUser handshake to log a nearby device in. The official/legitimate transmitter path for third parties is the Web API's player endpoints plus the app SDKs. Note the important nuance: transferring playback does NOT stream audio from the transmitter — it only redirects which cloud-fed device decodes the stream.

name: Sonos
category: multi-room-audio ecosystem; control+streaming (transport-substrate for local UPnP/SOAP control, cloud REST control API, music-service handoff via SMAPI, and AirPlay 2 / Spotify Connect as ingest paths)
summary: Sonos is a proprietary multi-room wireless audio ecosystem. Its players form an AES-encrypted peer-to-peer mesh (SonosNet) and were historically built on UPnP AV: each player exposes a MediaRenderer/MediaServer with UPnP services (AVTransport, RenderingControl, ZoneGroupTopology, ContentDirectory, MusicServices) reachable via SOAP over HTTP on port 1400. Sonos now offers an official cloud-mediated REST Control API and pushes third parties toward it, while the local UPnP/SOAP surface remains undocumented, unsupported, and is being gradually deprecated in the post-2024 S2 app. Music services integrate through SMAPI, a documented SOAP/WSDL API. Sonos also acts as an ingest sink for AirPlay 2 and Spotify Connect on supported hardware.
transmitterPlatforms: Sonos app (iOS/Android/desktop) as primary controller - post-2024 rewrite favors newer Sonos APIs over UPnP/SOAP
Third-party controllers via the local UPnP/SOAP API on port 1400 (SoCo Python, node-sonos-http-api, openHAB/Home Assistant bindings) - unofficial/unsupported
Third-party cloud integrations via the official REST Control API (OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens, api.ws.sonos.com)
Music services acting as content sources implement SMAPI (SOAP server that Sonos calls into)
Apple devices as AirPlay 2 senders; Spotify app as Spotify Connect controller; UPnP/DLNA control points via OpenHome (BubbleUPnP)
receiverPlatforms: Sonos hardware players are the receivers/sinks (Play/One/Five/Beam/Arc/Move/Roam/Port/Amp etc.)
As UPnP AV MediaRenderer: accepts AVTransport SetAVTransportURI to stream HTTP/streaming URLs
As OpenHome renderer: interoperates with BubbleUPnP and OpenHome control points (better than raw DLNA)
As AirPlay 2 receiver: on Sonos One, 2nd-gen Play:5, Playbase, Beam, and all newer S2 hardware (older/underpowered models like Play:1, Play:3, original Play:5 cannot)
As Spotify Connect endpoint: most current players

Building an OPEN third-party receiver that impersonates a Sonos player is not a documented/supported path - the interesting open-receiver targets here are the underlying AirPlay 2 and UPnP/DLNA protocols Sonos itself ingests
howItWorks: Discovery historically via SSDP (UPnP) and mDNS; each player hosts device/service description XML at http://<ip>:1400/xml/*.xml. Control is SOAP 1.1 over HTTP to endpoints like /MediaRenderer/AVTransport/Control with a SOAPACTION header. Grouping is a first-class Sonos concept layered on UPnP: one player becomes the group coordinator (identified by a RINCON URN); SetAVTransportURI to another player's RINCON joins it to that coordinator's group, and AVTransport actions like BecomeCoordinatorOfStandaloneGroup/DelegateGroupCoordinationTo manage topology. ZoneGroupTopology reports the household layout; UPnP eventing (GENA callbacks) delivers state changes. Playback is coordinator-driven queue management: the coordinator fetches content (direct HTTP streams, or via a music service) and syncs playback across grouped players over SonosNet. The official cloud Control API instead routes everything through Sonos's cloud gateway: an OAuth 2.0 flow (getAuthCode/createToken/refreshToken, scope playback-control-all) yields a bearer token; clients issue REST calls (e.g. POST /groups/{groupId}/playback/play) and receive asynchronous state via a WebSocket/webhook event channel that the developer registers. A local variant of the Control API on the LAN exists but Sonos states it is not for wide release. Music services plug in via SMAPI: Sonos is the SOAP client and calls the service's WSDL-described SOAP endpoint (getMetadata, getMediaURI, search, etc.) to browse catalogs and resolve stream URLs, with a separate auth handshake (see auth field).

authEncryption: Local UPnP/SOAP control has historically been essentially unauthenticated on the LAN (any device on the network can issue SOAP actions to port 1400) - this is a big reason it's easy to reverse-engineer but also why Sonos is moving away from it. SonosNet inter-player traffic is AES-encrypted (proprietary). The official cloud Control API uses OAuth 2.0 authorization-code flow with bearer access/refresh tokens; developers register an integration and API key with Sonos. SMAPI supports several auth models: Anonymous, Application Link (App Link, callback-based user linking), Device Link Code (user enters a code), Device Auth Token / Session ID, and a newer recommended OAuth path. AirPlay 2 ingest requires Apple's stack: HomeKit transient pairing (SRP + Curve25519 + ChaCha20-Poly1305) plus FairPlay (v3) authentication and AES key exchange to decrypt the audio - this FairPlay handshake is the primary DRM/link-protection blocker for any open AirPlay 2 receiver.

protocolDocs: Mixed. SMAPI is officially and publicly documented (docs.sonos.com/docs/smapi, developer.sonos.com), including downloadable WSDL/XSD - fully open to implement as a music-service provider. The cloud Control API is officially documented (docs.sonos.com/reference/about-control-api) with sample apps (github.com/sonos/api-web-sample-app). The local UPnP/SOAP control API is NOT officially documented or supported by Sonos; the authoritative community references are svrooij's sonos-api-docs (sonos.svrooij.io) and the SoCo wiki, both derived from device service-discovery XML and reverse engineering. The AirPlay 2 protocol Sonos ingests is not officially published; the key reverse-engineering writeups are emanuelecozzi.net/docs/airplay2 (AirPlay 2 Internals) and the openairplay/shairport-sync codebases.
receiverFeasibility: Two very different "receiver" framings must not be conflated. (1) Building an open device that impersonates a Sonos player (so the Sonos app/other players treat it as a sink): not a documented or supported path, would require reimplementing SonosNet (AES-encrypted proprietary mesh), the ZoneGroupTopology/coordinator model, and evolving firmware handshakes - effectively adversarial reverse engineering with no license; high effort and fragile. Nobody maintains a serious open "fake Sonos player." (2) Building an open receiver for the protocols Sonos itself ingests is far more tractable and is where the ecosystem already is: as a UPnP-AV/OpenHome MediaRenderer this is straightforward (well-understood UPnP), and Sonos-as-renderer already works with BubbleUPnP; as an AirPlay 2 sink it is feasible but blocked by FairPlay v3 + HomeKit pairing crypto, which shairport-sync and openairplay/airplay2-receiver have reverse-engineered (with limitations). Net: an open receiver for standard UPnP/DLNA is easy; an open AirPlay 2 receiver is medium-hard with the FairPlay/HomeKit handshake as the main blocker; an open Sonos-native receiver is impractical.
transmitterNotes: Transmitter (controller) side is the well-trodden path. Local control: SoCo, node-sonos-http-api, and svrooij's docs give reliable coverage of AVTransport/RenderingControl/ZoneGroupTopology over SOAP on port 1400 - easy to build against today, but Sonos is gradually removing UPnP features in the S2 app, so this is a decaying surface with future-breakage risk. Cloud control: the official REST Control API is stable and supported but requires OAuth, a registered developer key, routes through Sonos's cloud (added latency/dependency), and is content-limited (Favorites/playlists/cloud-queue/stream URLs rather than deep catalog browse). To be a content source rather than a controller, implement SMAPI (SOAP/WSDL) - documented and open, requiring a Content Integration Form submission and Sonos review before production. For pushing audio into Sonos without any Sonos-specific code, use it as an AirPlay 2 or Spotify Connect endpoint, or send it a plain HTTP stream URL via SetAVTransportURI.

name: Matter Casting
aka: Matter Casting (Matter Video Player / Content App architecture)
category: app-launch / app-specific-handoff (deep-link + remote-control casting). NOT screen-mirroring and NOT media-URL-pixel-streaming from the sender. Rides on the Matter smart-home stack as its transport/commissioning substrate.
summary: Matter Casting is the Connectivity Standards Alliance (CSA) casting model built on top of Matter's media ("Application") clusters. A phone/tablet/PC app (the "Casting Client") discovers a TV or smart display (the "Casting Player"), joins it on a Matter fabric via commissioning, then sends cluster commands (ContentLauncher, MediaPlayback, etc.) telling a content app ALREADY on the TV to fetch and play content from its own backend. It is a control-plane / app-handoff protocol, not a pixel or media stream from the sender — the receiver's app does the actual streaming and owns its own DRM. CSA positions it as a royalty-free, open, cross-ecosystem alternative to Google Cast and AirPlay, but as of 2025-2026 real-world use is almost entirely inside Amazon's ecosystem (Fire TV / Echo Show as receivers; Prime Video and, from Dec 2025, Tubi as senders).
transmitterPlatforms: iOS and Android apps via the open-source Matter TV Casting library (tv-casting-app) in project-chip/connectedhomeip; Linux reference client also exists
In production, Amazon Prime Video (iOS/Android) is the flagship sender; Tubi launched as a sender on Fire TV around Dec 2025

Any app can in principle become a Casting Client by embedding the tv-casting-app library, but must be CSA-certified and vendor-authorized by the target content apps (DAC vendor match) to actually cast into them
Sender platforms are the phone/tablet/PC; there is no OS-level 'cast from anywhere' surface like Chromecast's — it is per-app integration
receiverPlatforms: Amazon Fire TV devices (Fire OS 7+): Fire TV Stick 4K/Max, 3rd-gen Fire TV Cube, and Fire TV OS smart TVs — production receivers
Amazon Echo Show 15 / Echo Show (smart displays) — first shipping receiver (spring 2024)
Panasonic TVs with Fire TV OS built-in — announced/rolling out via the Amazon partnership
Reference open-source receiver: the 'tv-app' (Matter Video Player + Content App Platform) in project-chip/connectedhomeip, Linux/Raspberry Pi, demonstration-grade with hardcoded dummy content apps
Announced-but-not-shipped (as of the 2024-2025 sources): Hisense, LG, TCL, Toshiba said they'd support it, none confirmed shipping
howItWorks: Roles: the sender is the 'Casting Client' (Matter Commissionee); the TV/display is the 'Casting Player' (Matter Commissioner) that hosts the 'Video Player' endpoint plus one or more 'Content App' endpoints. (1) DISCOVERY: the client finds Casting Players on the LAN via DNS-SD / mDNS (standard Matter commissionable-node discovery) and gets deviceName/vendorId/productId. (2) COMMISSIONING: the client sends a User Directed Commissioning (UDC) request; the player either displays a 4-6 digit passcode the user types into the client (Method 1), or the target content app returns a setup PIN programmatically via the Account Login cluster's GetSetupPIN (Method 2, using a Rotating ID / token round-tripped to the app's cloud). A PASE→CASE exchange establishes a secure session and joins the client to the player's Matter fabric. (3) AUTHORIZATION: the client presents its Device Attestation Certificate (DAC); the player reads the vendor from the DAC and matches it against the list of authorized client-vendors each content app declares, deciding which content apps this client may cast into. (4) RECONNECT: the client caches player info and later skips full UDC, just re-establishing a CASE session. (5) LAUNCH & CONTROL: the client selects an endpoint (a specific content app) and issues cluster commands — ContentLauncher (LaunchURL / LaunchContent to open the app and play a specific title, and can prompt install via ApplicationID/package name if missing), MediaPlayback (play/pause/skip/seek), ApplicationLauncher/ApplicationBasic, KeypadInput, TargetNavigator. The content app on the TV then streams the actual bytes from its own service. The player platform may either bridge existing internal app interfaces to Matter (apps stay non-Matter-aware) or expose Matter interfaces so apps respond to clusters directly.

Matter operational transport over IPv6/UDP on Wi-Fi/Ethernet (Matter Message Layer)

Actual A/V is delivered out-of-band by the content app: HLS/DASH over HTTPS from the app's CDN (not carried by Matter)
authEncryption: Auth/commissioning is standard Matter: PASE bootstrapped by a passcode (typed by user, or fetched from the content app cloud via Account Login GetSetupPIN), upgrading to a CASE session with certificate-based mutual auth and per-message AES encryption on the fabric. Device identity uses the Matter certificate chain (DAC/PAI/PAA) and Node Operational Certificates. Crucially for casting, the client's DAC vendor is used as an ACCESS-CONTROL signal: content apps whitelist which client vendors may cast into them, so Prime Video can restrict who launches it. There is NO Matter-Casting-specific DRM or link-encryption for the media itself — content protection (Widevine, FairPlay, PlayReady, etc.) is entirely the receiving content app's responsibility because the app streams the content directly from its own backend; Matter only secures the control channel and the commissioning/attestation handshake.

protocolDocs: Official and PUBLIC. The behavior is defined in the CSA 'Matter Application Cluster Specification' (media clusters + Video Player/Content App device types) and the Matter Core Specification (commissioning, PASE/CASE, DNS-SD, attestation), both freely downloadable from csa-iot.org (versions 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4). The SDK (project-chip/connectedhomeip) provides open reference code and per-platform READMEs/APIs.md for both tv-casting-app (sender) and tv-app (receiver). Amazon publishes developer-facing 'Overview of Matter Casting' and 'Matter Casting Integration' docs describing the real content-app/authorization flow. No reverse-engineering is needed — this is an open standard; the closed parts are vendor platform integrations and certification, not the wire protocol.
receiverFeasibility: Building an open receiver is architecturally feasible and there IS an open reference (connectedhomeip tv-app), but there are real gaps. The Matter/commissioning machinery (DNS-SD, UDC, PASE/CASE, DAC handling) is fully open and reusable. The hard/soft blockers: (1) It is a CONTROL protocol — your receiver must ALSO be, or must bridge to, real content apps that can stream and decrypt their own protected content; Matter gives you 'app X, play title Y', not the media. So an 'open receiver' is only as useful as the content apps you can host, and mainstream apps (Prime Video, Netflix, etc.) will not run on an unsanctioned device because they require app-level DRM (Widevine L1/FairPlay) + their own certification/business deals. (2) The reference tv-app ships dummy content apps with no actual playback. (3) DAC-based vendor authorization means content apps can refuse clients whose vendor isn't whitelisted; conversely a receiver you build won't be trusted by production senders unless certified. (4) Interop certification: to be a 'Matter Casting' receiver that certified senders will talk to, you generally need CSA certification and a real DAC from an attestation authority. (5) AUDIO-ONLY casting is essentially unspecified today — the shipped architecture is video-centric (Video Player device type); there are no ratified audio-player endpoints/device types and no multi-room audio sync in Matter, which is why community projects (music-assistant, ESPHome, wyoming-satellite) want it but none exists. Net: you can stand up an open receiver that commissions and receives control commands over a weekend using the SDK; making it play real premium content is blocked by app DRM + certification, not by the protocol being secret.
transmitterNotes: Transmitter side is the more tractable open target: the tv-casting-app library is a maintained, cross-platform (Linux/Android/iOS) open sender that handles discovery, UDC, CASE, and cluster invocation. You can build an app that discovers Casting Players and sends LaunchURL/LaunchContent + playback controls without reverse engineering. However, to cast INTO a specific commercial content app you must be authorized: the content app checks your client vendor (via DAC) against its whitelist, and to reach production Fire TV receivers you'd want CSA certification and a legitimate DAC. For a hobby/self-hosted target (your own receiver + your own content app), you fully control both ends and none of the authorization is a blocker. There is no OS-level 'cast this tab/screen' entry point — casting is per-app by design.

contestedClaims.claim: There is a distinct standalone document called 'the Matter Casting spec'.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Commonly said in press, but technically Matter Casting is not a separate spec — it is the set of media clusters and the Video Player / Content App device types defined within the CSA Matter Application Cluster Specification (plus core Matter for commissioning). 'Matter Casting' is a marketing/feature name, not a separate standard document. Worth stating precisely.

contestedClaims.claim: Matter Casting reuses/wraps Google Cast's Widevine and AirPlay 2's FairPlay DRM (as one comparison article claimed).
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: This claim comes from a marketing/SEO-flavored source (ampvortex) and appears to be wrong. Matter Casting is DRM-agnostic and has no DRM of its own; content protection is handled independently by each receiving content app's own player stack. It does NOT bridge into or depend on Google Cast or AirPlay DRM frameworks. Flagging as likely misreported.

contestedClaims.claim: Matter Casting streams audio/video from the sender to the receiver.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Frequently implied by 'casting' language and by comparisons to Chromecast. In reality the sender does NOT stream media (no pixel mirroring, no media proxy); it sends control/launch commands and the receiver's own app pulls the content from its backend. This is the single most commonly confused point and central to the receiver-build question.

contestedClaims.claim: Matter Casting supports audio-only / music casting and multi-room audio today.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: As of 2025-2026 the shipped architecture is video-centric; audio-player device types are not ratified and Matter explicitly does not provide multi-room audio sync. CSA working-group effort on audio use cases was described as nascent. Some marketing copy says 'audio and video' aspirationally — the audio path is not really usable yet.

contestedClaims.claim: Panasonic/LG/TCL/Hisense/Toshiba TVs ship Matter Casting receivers.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: These were announcements/intentions (mostly 2024). Only Amazon's own devices (Fire TV, Echo Show) and Fire-TV-OS-based sets (Panasonic partnership) are confirmed shipping; the others' shipping status by 2026 is uncertain and should be re-verified.

contestedClaims.claim: Exact spec version currently deployed and what 1.4 changed for casting.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Sources indicate Fire TV/Echo run on Matter 1.3 for casting and that 1.4 added 'barely any' casting changes (stability/perf), while Amazon was certifying a 1.4 update. The precise deployed version per device and the delta are version-sensitive and may have moved by mid-2026.

variants: By Matter spec version: media clusters exist since Matter 1.0; casting-relevant refinements in 1.2 (Oct 2023), 1.3 (push messages/dialog, casting init improvements, text/track support, search — 2024), and 1.4 (Nov 2024, mostly stability/perf for casting)

confidence: Medium-high. The architecture, roles, discovery/commissioning (DNS-SD, UDC, PASE/CASE), the app-handoff/deep-link content model, DAC-based authorization, the open reference implementations (tv-casting-app / tv-app), and Amazon-centric adoption are all corroborated across primary Amazon developer docs, the connectedhomeip SDK docs, and the CSA spec, plus secondary press. Lower confidence on exact per-device deployed spec versions in mid-2026 and on non-Amazon TV vendor shipping status, which are time-sensitive. The 'no DRM of its own / DRM is the content app's job' point is well-supported by the shape of the protocol but is not spelled out verbatim in a single primary DRM doc, hence flagged.

name: Roku ECP and Amazon Fling/Whisperplay
category: Two distinct families: (1) Roku ECP = app-launch + remote-control + media-URL-launch over SSDP+REST, with DIAL as a secondary app-launch target and Miracast/AirPlay2 as separate screen-mirroring stacks. (2) Amazon Fling/Whisperplay = media-URL-fling + second-screen control over a proprietary Thrift-based substrate, with DIAL for app-launch and Miracast for mirroring. Spans: app-launch, media-URL-casting, app-specific-handoff, screen-mirroring, and a transport-substrate (Whisperplay).
summary: Roku ECP (External Control Protocol) is a simple, open, unauthenticated LAN control API: SSDP for discovery plus a plaintext HTTP/REST service on port 8060 for remote keypresses, app launch/query, media-player status, and deep-linked media-URL launch. Roku separately acts as a DIAL app-launch target and (on many models) a Miracast/AirPlay-2 screen-mirroring sink; these are three different mechanisms, not one. Amazon Fling is a media-URL-flinging + second-screen SDK for Fire TV built on Amazon's proprietary Whisperplay/WhisperLink substrate (Apache Thrift over HTTP); Fire TV separately supports DIAL app-launch (implemented via Whisperplay) and, on some models, Miracast mirroring. Fling reached end-of-support on 2026-03-05 with Amazon steering developers to Matter Casting.

Roku screen mirroring: Miracast (Wi-Fi Direct) sink on many models; separate AirPlay 2 sink on newer models

Roku DIAL: any DIAL client (mobile apps like Netflix/YouTube) can launch registered apps

Fire TV receiver (DIAL + Fling player): Fire TV Stick/Cube/Fire TV Edition devices running Fire OS with the Whisperplay service; Fling requires a developer-built 'player' app installed on the Fire TV plus the platform Whisperplay layer

AirPlay 2 sink: AirPlay-2-capable Roku models

Open/DIY receivers: an open Miracast sink is achievable on Linux (MiracleCast/OpenWFD) with suitable Wi-Fi hardware; an open ECP/DIAL receiver is trivial to build (plain HTTP+SSDP) but has no widely-used complete open implementation; an open Fling/Whisperplay receiver is effectively blocked by the proprietary Thrift RPC substrate and SID registration
howItWorks: Roku ECP: A controller sends an SSDP M-SEARCH (multicast 239.255.255.250:1900) with ST 'roku:ecp'; the Roku replies with a LOCATION header pointing at http://<ip>:8060/ and a USN of 'uuid:roku:ecp:<serial>'. The controller then issues plain HTTP REST calls to port 8060: POST /keypress/<Key> (Home, Select, arrows, and Lit_<char> for keyboard), POST /launch/<appId>?<deeplink params> (app launch, optionally with contentId/mediaType to jump straight to a media asset = 'media-URL launch'), POST /install/<appId>, GET /query/apps, GET /query/device-info, GET /query/media-player (playback state), plus POST /input and /search. No cast/mirror session is negotiated - ECP just tells an app what to do; the app fetches its own stream. Roku DIAL: separate SSDP ST 'urn:dial-multiscreen-org:service:dial:1' yields an APPLICATION-URL; a DIAL client does GET (status) / POST (launch) on /apps/<AppName>. Roku Miracast/AirPlay are wholly separate real-time media pipelines. Amazon Fling: the Fling SDK's DiscoveryController finds RemoteMediaPlayer objects advertised by SID over the LAN (Whisperplay); the controller connects and calls setMediaSource(url,...) to fling a media URL, then play/pause/seek and receive status callbacks. Amazon DIAL on Fire TV is layered on Whisperplay (whisperplay.xml declares the DIAL app name and authorizedOrigins for CORS/additionalDataUrl). Under Fling and Amazon-DIAL sits WhisperLink: an Apache Thrift RPC service reached by HTTP POST to a /whisperlink path with Thrift-binary-encoded function calls (per reverse-engineering sources). Miracast on both is 'HDMI over Wi-Fi': Wi-Fi Direct pairing then an RTSP-negotiated H.264/MPEG-TS video stream.

Wi-Fi Direct / Wi-Fi P2P (Miracast link layer)

mDNS/Bonjour (used by AirPlay discovery; NOT used by ECP, which uses SSDP)
authEncryption: Roku ECP: essentially NO authentication and NO transport encryption - plaintext HTTP on the LAN. The only gate is an on-device toggle 'Control by mobile apps' (enforced for most commands as of Roku OS 14.1); developer-only ECP commands (chanperf, sgnodes, registry, etc.) additionally require developer mode. There is no pairing handshake or API key. Roku DIAL: no auth in the protocol itself; the spec warns that launch payloads come from untrusted sources and must be validated by the app. Roku Miracast: Wi-Fi Direct pairing (often WPS-style PIN/push), optional HDCP 2.x link encryption; a PIN is shown on-screen. Roku AirPlay 2: Apple's pairing with an on-screen code. Amazon Fling/Whisperplay: the Whisperplay/WhisperLink Thrift-over-HTTP substrate is proprietary but not strongly authenticated at the app level in the classic model; Amazon-DIAL uses an authorizedOrigins (CORS-origin allowlist) in whisperplay.xml to gate who may POST additionalData. Fire TV Miracast: Wi-Fi Direct pairing plus optional HDCP. In short: the biggest 'auth' blockers for a would-be sink are not crypto but (a) Wi-Fi-Direct/HDCP for Miracast and (b) the closed Thrift SID substrate for Fling.

protocolDocs: Roku ECP: OFFICIAL and PUBLIC - developer.roku.com/dev/docs/external-control-api (and the sdkdocs-archive mirror). Full endpoint list, SSDP details, and the OS-14.1 'Control by mobile apps' gating are documented. DIAL: OFFICIAL and PUBLIC - dial-multiscreen.org publishes the spec (v1.6.4 through v2.2.x PDFs) plus an app-name registry and developer notes; co-developed by Netflix/Google (with Sony/Samsung). Amazon Fling: OFFICIAL developer docs at developer.amazon.com/docs/fling (Android/iOS integration, MediaRouter, Unity, Fire TV player), but they describe the SDK, not the wire protocol. Amazon DIAL-on-Fire-TV: documented at developer.amazon.com/docs/fire-tv/dial-integration.html (whisperplay.xml, authorizedOrigins, additionalDataUrl). Whisperplay/WhisperLink wire format: NO official public spec - it is REVERSE-ENGINEERED-ONLY; the Thrift-over-HTTP /whisperlink description appears in secondary/security writeups (notably a Bitdefender Fire TV vulnerability whitepaper, 2023). Miracast/WFD: Wi-Fi-Alliance spec is licensed/not fully public; the open OpenWFD/MiracleCast projects and FOSDEM 2014 talks are the practical open references.
receiverFeasibility: Three very different difficulty tiers. (1) Roku ECP receiver = EASY. It is just an SSDP responder + a plaintext HTTP server on 8060 implementing a handful of REST routes; no crypto, no pairing. A systems engineer could stand up a faithful ECP/DIAL sink in a weekend. The catch: real Roku controllers expect specific query XML shapes and app-launch semantics, and there is no polished open receiver today (python-roku's 'emulator' is a stub), so you'd implement from the docs. (2) Miracast sink (what people mean by 'screen mirroring to Roku/Fire TV') = MODERATE-HARD but PROVEN open. MiracleCast shows it's doable on Linux, but you need Wi-Fi hardware supporting Wi-Fi Direct/P2P and softAP, a working wpa_supplicant P2P + RTSP/RTP/H.264 decode pipeline, and you must handle Wi-Fi-Direct pairing; HDCP-protected content is a hard blocker unless you have an HDCP-licensed path. (3) Amazon Fling/Whisperplay receiver = HARD/BLOCKED. The substrate is a proprietary Apache-Thrift RPC (/whisperlink) with Amazon service identifiers and no public spec; you'd be fully reverse-engineering, there is no open implementation, and Amazon has EOL'd Fling (2026-03-05) in favor of Matter Casting - so effort here is high and future-value low. Net advice for an open sink: implement ECP + DIAL directly (open, trivial), reuse MiracleCast for mirroring, and treat Fling/Whisperplay as not worth targeting.
transmitterNotes: Transmitter side is much easier across the board. Roku ECP: no SDK, no auth handshake - just POST to http://<roku>:8060/keypress/... and /launch/...; many small open clients exist (python-rokuecp, python-roku, C rokuecp, Ruby, Rust crates). Media-URL 'casting' to Roku is done by /launch/<appId>?contentId=...&mediaType=... which deep-links into an installed channel (the channel fetches the stream itself) - it is NOT a generic 'push any URL' cast and NOT mirroring. Roku DIAL transmitter: standard DIAL client behavior (how Netflix/YouTube phones launch the TV app). Amazon Fling transmitter: use the (now EOL) Fling SDK on Android/iOS - DiscoveryController to find RemoteMediaPlayer by SID, then setMediaSource + transport controls; also an Android MediaRouter provider and Unity plugin. Miracast/AirPlay source: use the OS's built-in wireless-display/AirPlay UI. Key transmitter caveat: because ECP is unauthenticated, anything on the LAN can control a Roku - convenient for building tools, but also the reason Roku added the 'Control by mobile apps' toggle.

name: WebRTC and browser-based casting (Presentation API, Remote Playback API, Chrome Cast mirroring, Open Screen Protocol)
aka: W3C Second Screen APIs (Presentation API + Remote Playback API)
category: A cluster of related browser-based screen/media casting mechanisms: (1) app-launch + media-URL casting (Cast/DIAL), (2) screen-mirroring (Cast Streaming RTP; and separately WebRTC), (3) browser web-standard control APIs (Presentation API = app-launch/handoff, Remote Playback API = media-element remoting), (4) a would-be open transport-substrate + successor protocol (Open Screen Protocol). WebRTC itself is a peer-to-peer low-latency transport, not a casting-to-sink protocol.
summary: "Browser-based casting" is really several distinct things that are frequently conflated. Google Cast (Chromecast) supports two very different modes: media-URL casting, where the sender just hands a receiver app a content URL plus playback commands and the receiver fetches/plays it itself (like DIAL app-launch, high quality, low sender load); and screen/tab mirroring, where the sender captures, encodes and streams live pixels to the receiver. Chrome's Chromecast mirroring uses "Cast Streaming," a custom RTP/RTCP media path with AES keys negotiated in a JSON offer/answer over the CastV2 control channel — this is Cast-specific and is commonly and incorrectly described as "WebRTC." Real WebRTC (getDisplayMedia + RTCPeerConnection, DTLS-SRTP, ICE) is a separate peer-to-peer screen-sharing transport used between browsers/apps, not a way to reach a Chromecast sink. The web-standard control surfaces are the Presentation API (launch/handoff arbitrary web content to a second display and message it) and the Remote Playback API (remote a single <video>/<audio> element). The Open Screen Protocol (OSP) is W3C's royalty-free, QUIC/TLS-based network protocol intended to let independent vendors implement those two APIs interoperably — a potential open successor to Cast/DIAL, but with limited real-world adoption.
transmitterPlatforms: Chrome/Chromium desktop: built-in Cast sender for tab casting, desktop/screen mirroring, and media-URL casting to Chromecast/Cast-enabled devices; also Cast Web Sender SDK for websites (Cast button)
Chrome on Android: Cast integration plus Remote Playback API for <video>
Android OS: system 'Cast screen' mirroring, and native Cast SDK (Android Sender) in apps
iOS: Google Cast iOS Sender SDK (media-URL casting; no OS-level mirroring to Cast)
Any browser implementing Presentation API / Remote Playback API as a Controlling User Agent (Chromium-family primarily; Safari maps Remote Playback to AirPlay; Firefox largely does not ship these)
WebRTC senders: any browser/app using getDisplayMedia()+RTCPeerConnection (peer-to-peer, requires your own signaling+receiver, not a Cast sink)
For OSP specifically: intended to be any browser Controlling User Agent; in practice near-zero shipping transmitters
receiverPlatforms: Chromecast / Google Cast built-in devices, Android TV / Google TV, Nest displays/speakers (closed, HW-key authenticated Cast receivers)

howItWorks: "Discovery: Cast devices advertise over mDNS/DNS-SD (Chromecast historically also used SSDP/DIAL for app discovery). OSP uses mDNS/DNS-SD under the _openscreen._udp service. Sender picks a device. Control: Cast opens a TLS connection to the device on TCP 8009 and speaks CastV2 — length-prefixed Protobuf messages on named namespaces (urn:x-cast:com.google.cast.*), including device-auth, connection, receiver (launch app), and media namespaces. Media-URL casting: sender uses the media namespace (loadMedia with a MediaInformation URL + MediaStatus updates); the receiver app fetches and plays the content itself — the sender only sends control messages, not pixels. Mirroring (Cast Streaming): sender launches the mirroring receiver, then negotiates a JSON Offer/Answer (codecs, resolutions, AES key + IV mask, RTP SSRCs, receiver UDP port) over the CastV2 control channel, then streams encoded VP8/H.264 video + Opus/AAC audio as AES-encrypted RTP/RTCP over UDP with Cast-specific framing and feedback for congestion/latency adaptation. This is NOT DTLS-SRTP/ICE WebRTC. WebRTC (separate world): getDisplayMedia() captures a tab/screen -> RTCPeerConnection with SDP offer/answer over your own signaling channel -> ICE (STUN/TURN) path selection -> DTLS handshake -> SRTP-encrypted media peer-to-peer. Presentation API: Controlling UA calls PresentationRequest with URL(s); receiving UA loads that web content on the second display; a PresentationConnection carries app-defined messages both ways. Remote Playback API: HTMLMediaElement.remote.prompt() picks a device and remotes just that element (play/pause/seek/state), which is why it's easier to standardize than full presentation. OSP maps both APIs onto QUIC+TLS1.3 connections carrying CBOR messages, with SPAKE2-based pairing to establish trust; media streaming in OSP is negotiated similarly (capabilities/codec exchange from the WebCodecs registry)."

authEncryption: "Cast control (CastV2): runs over TLS. Cast Device Authentication is the key receiver blocker: on connect the sender issues a challenge; the receiver must sign it with a per-device private key that is fused into the device SoC (not extractable in software), presenting a certificate chain Device cert -> Intermediate CA -> Google Root CA. Senders verify this chain. It is technically optional from the sender's perspective, but official senders (Chrome, mobile Cast SDKs) enforce it and drop connections that fail — so a from-scratch open receiver cannot be authenticated by official senders without a genuine device's fused key (Tristan Penman demonstrated bootstrapping it only by rooting a real 1st-gen Chromecast and signing with its hardware). Cast Streaming media: encrypted with AES-128 using an aes_key + aes_iv_mask delivered inside the Offer/Answer over the (TLS-protected) control channel — link protection, not content DRM. Media-URL casting: any content DRM (Widevine etc.) is handled by the receiver app via EME/CDM when it fetches the stream; not part of the cast handshake. WebRTC: mandatory DTLS-SRTP media encryption with keys from the DTLS handshake; certificates are typically self-signed and verified out-of-band via signaling. OSP: self-signed X.509 (P-256 ECDSA) identities, TLS 1.3 over QUIC, trust established via SPAKE2 pairing with a low-entropy user-entered PSK (>=20 bits default); OSP spec does not define its own content DRM."

protocolDocs: "Mixed. PUBLIC/official: W3C specs for the Presentation API and Remote Playback API; the Open Screen Protocol spec (application + network protocols) is a public W3C Second Screen WG document with editor's drafts into 2026; openscreen library source and its cast/streaming and cast/protocol READMEs are public and describe the Cast Streaming offer/answer + RTP model and the CastV2 message layout. Google's Cast SDK developer docs (senders, CAF Web Receiver, media namespace messages) are public. WebRTC is fully standardized (W3C WebRTC 1.0 + IETF RTCWEB RFCs). REVERSE-ENGINEERED-ONLY / not officially published as an open spec: the full CastV2 wire protocol details and especially the Device Authentication scheme — documented mainly via community teardowns (Tristan Penman's Chromecast device-authentication writeup, OakBits Google Cast protocol overview, node-castv2 project docs, various blog teardowns). The Cast device-auth PKI and the fused device keys are proprietary and undocumented publicly."
receiverFeasibility: "Depends entirely on which mode you target. (1) Cast media-URL / control receiver that OFFICIAL senders accept: effectively blocked. You'd need to pass Cast Device Authentication, which requires a per-device private key fused into a genuine Cast SoC and a cert chain to Google's Root CA. Only route shown in the wild is extracting keys from a rootable real device (1st-gen Chromecast) — not a general solution and not shippable. (2) Cast Streaming (mirroring) receiver: the media path itself is open and reproducible — offer/answer JSON, AES-128 keys handed to you in that negotiation, custom RTP/RTCP over UDP, VP8/H.264+Opus/AAC — and openscreen ships a standalone_receiver you can study/run. But to be reached by Chrome's mirroring you still sit behind the CastV2 control channel and its device auth, so a non-authenticated receiver won't be selected by stock senders. (3) OSP receiver: architecturally the friendliest to build openly — royalty-free spec, QUIC/TLS1.3, CBOR, SPAKE2 user-PIN pairing (no vendor key/cert authority to gatekeep), openscreen provides receiver code — but there is essentially no installed base of OSP senders, so an OSP sink has little to talk to today. (4) WebRTC 'receiver': trivial and fully open, but it's your own peer with your own signaling, not a standardized casting sink discoverable by browsers. Bottom line: the auth PKI (not codecs or transport) is the real blocker for a Cast sink; OSP removes that blocker but lacks adoption; WebRTC is open but is a different problem shape."
transmitterNotes: "Sender side is far more open. Media-URL casting and app launch can be driven by mature reverse-engineered/official libraries (pychromecast, node-castv2, Google Cast SDKs). Note that Cast Device Authentication protects the *sender verifying the receiver*, not the receiver verifying the sender — so an unofficial *sender* talking to a genuine Chromecast is generally fine (auth is optional from the sender's side), which is why pychromecast-style control works. Building an unofficial *mirroring sender* (Cast Streaming source) is feasible using openscreen's standalone_sender / cast/streaming code. Remote Playback API and Presentation API senders are just standard browser APIs (Chromium-family; Safari routes Remote Playback to AirPlay). For OSP, transmitter code exists in openscreen but there's little ecosystem to send to. WebRTC transmitters (getDisplayMedia + RTCPeerConnection) are trivial but require you to also run signaling and your own receiving peer."

contestedClaims.claim: Chrome tab/desktop mirroring to a Chromecast uses WebRTC.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Very commonly stated (Android Authority, older bloggeek posts) but imprecise/likely wrong as usually meant. Chrome mirroring uses Cast Streaming — a custom RTP/RTCP path with AES keys from a JSON offer/answer over CastV2 — NOT standard WebRTC RTCPeerConnection/DTLS-SRTP/ICE. It borrows the *offer/answer concept* from WebRTC and shares some codec/capture machinery, and the openscreen mirroring code historically lived near WebRTC building blocks, which fuels the conflation. I'm confident it is not classic WebRTC transport, but the exact degree of shared internals in current Chrome is not fully documented publicly.

contestedClaims.claim: Cast Streaming media codecs are VP8/Opus.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: openscreen docs cite VP8 + Opus as baseline; but real Chrome mirroring commonly negotiates H.264 (and can do VP9/AV1) and AAC depending on device/build. Exact negotiated set is device- and version-dependent, so treating VP8/Opus as the only codecs would be wrong.

contestedClaims.claim: An open receiver simply cannot be authenticated by official Cast senders.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: True in practice for a from-scratch software receiver (needs SoC-fused device key + Google-CA-chained cert). But it has been bootstrapped by extracting keys from a rooted genuine 1st-gen Chromecast (Tristan Penman). So 'impossible' is too strong; 'not achievable without genuine Cast hardware secrets, and not shippable/scalable' is the accurate framing.

contestedClaims.claim: Cast device authentication proves the receiver to the sender (not the sender to the receiver).
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: This is my reading of the teardown (sender challenges receiver; receiver signs). It explains why unofficial senders work but unofficial receivers don't. I'm fairly confident but it's based on reverse-engineering writeups, not an official spec, and could have evolved across protocol versions.

contestedClaims.claim: Open Screen Protocol is a live successor to Cast/DIAL.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: It is a real, actively-edited W3C spec with a reference library, and was explicitly designed as a royalty-free alternative to Cast. But real-world sender/receiver adoption appears minimal, and it's unclear whether Chrome ships OSP as a user-facing casting path today. Calling it 'the successor' overstates current deployment; 'intended open successor, low adoption' is safer.

contestedClaims.claim: Chromecast uses SSDP/DIAL vs mDNS for discovery.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Both have been involved historically (DIAL/SSDP for app discovery/launch heritage; mDNS/DNS-SD for device discovery), and specifics have shifted across Chromecast generations. Exact current discovery stack for a given device/firmware is version-dependent.
