name: Lower-level transport and media substrate (for screen-mirroring / media-casting protocols)
summary: This dossier covers the shared substrate layers that casting/mirroring protocols (AirPlay, Google Cast, Miracast, DLNA) are built on, rather than a single protocol. It spans three functional strata: (1) service discovery (mDNS/DNS-SD, SSDP/UPnP, DIAL, Wi-Fi Direct/P2P), (2) session control and media transport (RTSP/RTP/RTCP, SRTP, MPEG-TS, HLS/DASH/CMAF, TLS/DTLS), and (3) codecs and link/content protection (H.264/HEVC/AV1, AAC/Opus/ALAC, plus HDCP, DTCP-IP, and DRM systems FairPlay/Widevine/PlayReady). For a receiver-builder, the discovery and transport layers are almost entirely open and implementable from RFCs; the hard blockers are all in the auth/pairing and link-protection strata, which rely on device-fused keys, licensed certificates, and secure hardware.
variants: Discovery family: mDNS/DNS-SD (Bonjour, RFC 6762/6763) vs SSDP/UPnP (multicast 239.255.255.250:1900) vs DIAL (SSDP+HTTP, DIAL-specific ST) vs Wi-Fi Direct/P2P (Wi-Fi Alliance) for infrastructure-less L2 links
Control/transport family: RTSP (RFC 2326/7826) session control + RTP/RTCP (RFC 3550) media, optionally SRTP (RFC 3711) for encryption; DTLS-SRTP used by WebRTC-style paths
Media packaging family: raw RTP payloads vs MPEG-2 Transport Stream (MPEG-TS, used by Miracast) vs HLS (M3U8 + TS or fMP4) vs MPEG-DASH (MPD + fMP4) vs unifying CMAF (ISO/IEC 23000-19)

Encryption/DRM scheme family: HDCP (link, HDMI/DP and HDCP 2.x over IP) vs DTCP-IP (link, home network) vs application DRM via CENC ISO/IEC 23001-7 with two modes: AES-CTR 'cenc' (Widevine/PlayReady) and AES-CBC 'cbcs' (FairPlay, and now cross-DRM)
Codec family: video H.264/AVC, H.265/HEVC, AV1; audio AAC-LC, AAC-ELD (low-delay, AirPlay mirroring), ALAC (Apple Lossless), Opus, PCM
transmitterPlatforms: Any OS can advertise/browse mDNS-DNS-SD (Apple Bonjour, Linux Avahi, Windows native mDNS) and SSDP/UPnP
iOS/macOS: native AirPlay sender stack (RAOP audio + mirroring) built on RTSP/RTP + FairPlay
Android/Chrome/Chromecast built-in: Google Cast sender SDK (CASTV2 over TLS), plus DIAL for app-launch
Windows/Android: Miracast source (Wi-Fi Direct + RTSP + RTP/MPEG-TS)
Servers/CDNs: HLS/DASH/CMAF origin packagers as the 'transmitter' for media-URL casting
receiverPlatforms: Linux/RPi/generic hosts running open receivers: shairport-sync (AirPlay/AirPlay 2 audio), UxPlay/RPiPlay (AirPlay mirroring), openairplay/airplay2-receiver (Python), PhairPlay (multi-protocol)
Linux Miracast sinks (require Wi-Fi Direct-capable chipset in P2P/softAP mode) via MiracleCast
DLNA/UPnP AV media renderers (Kodi, gmediarender, minidlna-ecosystem renderers) — fully open substrate
HLS/DASH: any player with mDNS/HTTP (VLC, ffmpeg, dash.js, hls.js, ExoPlayer, AVPlayer) acts as the 'sink' for URL-cast media
Google Cast receiver: effectively only Google-certified silicon (device cert blocker); Web Receiver runs as a hosted Chromium app
howItWorks: Discovery: senders find sinks via multicast. mDNS/DNS-SD queries a service type (e.g. _airplay._tcp, _raop._tcp, _googlecast._tcp) on 224.0.0.251:5353 and resolves SRV/TXT/A records; SSDP M-SEARCHes 239.255.255.250:1900 and dereferences a UPnP device/service XML description; DIAL layers an app-launch REST API over SSDP+HTTP; Wi-Fi Direct forms an ad-hoc L2 group when there's no shared LAN. Pairing/auth (the gate): varies per protocol — AirPlay uses HomeKit-style SRP + Curve25519/Ed25519 pairing plus FairPlay (/fp-setup) or MFi (/auth-setup) to unwrap AES media keys; Google Cast runs a CASTV2 device-authentication challenge over TLS requiring a Google-signed device certificate. Session setup: RTSP (AirPlay, Miracast) or a protobuf control channel (Cast) negotiates codecs, ports, timing, and keys. Streaming: media flows as RTP payloads (optionally SRTP), MPEG-TS-in-RTP (Miracast), or HTTP-pulled HLS/DASH/CMAF segments; A/V sync uses RTCP and/or an NTP-based clock (AirPlay). Link/content protection sits orthogonally: DRM (CENC-encrypted segments decrypted in a secure path) protects the content, while HDCP/DTCP-IP protect the wire/link to the display.
lowerLevelProtocols: mDNS (RFC 6762) / DNS-SD (RFC 6763) over UDP 5353, multicast 224.0.0.251 / ff02::fb
SSDP over UDP 1900, multicast 239.255.255.250; UPnP (device/service description over HTTP, SOAP control, GENA eventing)
DIAL (DIscovery And Launch = SSDP discovery + HTTP REST app-launch)
Wi-Fi Direct / Wi-Fi P2P (IEEE 802.11 + WPS/P2P), and Wi-Fi Display (WFD) service layer for Miracast
RTSP (RFC 2326 / RFC 7826) session control over TCP
RTP + RTCP (RFC 3550) media transport/statistics over UDP; SRTP (RFC 3711) for encrypted RTP
MPEG-2 Transport Stream (ISO/IEC 13818-1) as media container (Miracast, broadcast-style)
HLS (RFC 8216; M3U8 + MPEG-TS or fMP4) and MPEG-DASH (ISO/IEC 23009-1; MPD + fMP4) over HTTP(S)
CMAF (ISO/IEC 23000-19) fMP4 segments; CENC (ISO/IEC 23001-7) for common encryption
TLS (TCP, e.g. Cast on 8009) and DTLS (UDP) for control/key exchange; DTLS-SRTP keying
NTP / RTP timestamp clock for A/V synchronization
authEncryption: Three distinct and commonly-confused concerns. (1) Pairing/device-auth: proves who the peers are and unwraps session keys. AirPlay 2 uses HomeKit-style pairing (SRP-6a password/transient pair-setup, Curve25519 ECDH, Ed25519 signatures) plus FairPlay (POST /fp-setup, feature bit Authentication_4) or MFi (POST /auth-setup) chosen by feature flags; legacy RSA (Authentication_1) is disabled by Apple. Google Cast runs a CASTV2 challenge-response where the receiver must sign a hash of its TLS peer cert with a per-device private key fused into the SoC and return a cert chain up to Google's root CA. (2) Transport encryption: TLS (Cast control on 8009), DTLS/SRTP for RTP media in WebRTC-style paths, and AES media-key wrapping in AirPlay. (3) Content/link protection: DRM (FairPlay/Widevine/PlayReady) encrypts the media itself via CENC — 'cenc' AES-CTR (Widevine, PlayReady) vs 'cbcs' AES-CBC (FairPlay, now usable cross-DRM with CMAF); separately HDCP encrypts the physical/logical display link (HDMI/DisplayPort, and HDCP 2.x over IP for Miracast/streaming), and DTCP-IP encrypts links across a home IP network (DLNA). Critical distinction: HDCP and DTCP-IP are LINK protection (device-to-device wire), not DRM — they are enforced by DRM as a downstream chain-of-trust requirement but are separate mechanisms.

protocolDocs: Mixed and highly stratified. Substrate transport/discovery is OFFICIAL/PUBLIC: mDNS (RFC 6762), DNS-SD (RFC 6763), RTSP (RFC 2326/7826), RTP/RTCP (RFC 3550), SRTP (RFC 3711), HLS (RFC 8216), MPEG-DASH/CMAF/CENC (ISO/IEC 23009-1, 23000-19, 23001-7), plus published UPnP/DIAL specs and Wi-Fi Alliance Miracast overviews. The auth/pairing and link-protection layers are LICENSED-UNDER-NDA or REVERSE-ENGINEERED-ONLY: AirPlay 2 pairing/FairPlay is documented only through reverse-engineering (Emanuele Cozzi's 'AirPlay 2 Internals', the openairplay wiki, UxPlay/shairport-sync source, pyatv); Google Cast CASTV2 auth is documented via reverse-engineering writeups (Tristan Penman, Yingtong Li, dylanmckay/gcast PROTOCOL.md); HDCP/DTCP-IP/Widevine/PlayReady/FairPlay specs are all NDA. Key reverse-eng references: emanuelecozzi.net/docs/airplay2, github.com/openairplay, github.com/FDH2/UxPlay/wiki, tristanpenman.com Chromecast auth series.
receiverFeasibility: The feasibility gradient is sharp and layer-dependent. FEASIBLE/OPEN today: the whole discovery layer (mDNS/DNS-SD, SSDP/UPnP, DIAL) and the whole non-DRM media pipeline (RTSP/RTP/RTCP, MPEG-TS demux, HLS/DASH/CMAF fetching, H.264/HEVC/AV1 + AAC/Opus/ALAC decode) can be built from RFCs with GStreamer/FFmpeg. A DLNA/UPnP AV renderer or an unencrypted HLS/DASH sink is a solved problem. HARD BUT DONE (via reverse-eng, with legal grey areas): an AirPlay/AirPlay 2 receiver — shairport-sync (audio) and UxPlay (mirroring) prove it works, but they depend on redistributed Apple FairPlay blobs, so you inherit fragility (Apple can change feature bits/auth) and licensing risk rather than a clean license. EFFECTIVELY BLOCKED: a Google Cast receiver, because the CASTV2 challenge requires a per-device private key fused in the SoC and a Google-signed certificate chain a stock sender will trust — no open path to a valid cert; a Miracast sink for HDCP 2.x-protected sources; and any sink for DRM/HDCP/DTCP-IP-protected commercial content, which requires a licensed CDM and secure hardware (Widevine L1, PlayReady SL3000, FairPlay HW path) plus HDCP sink keys. Bottom line: build the transport/discovery/decode substrate open; expect the auth/pairing gate and the link-protection/DRM gate to be the two walls.
transmitterNotes: Transmitter side is markedly easier because the trust model runs receiver-proves-to-sender, not the reverse. Discovery advertising/browsing is trivial (Bonjour/Avahi). Google Cast SENDERS are well-served by open stacks (pychromecast, node-castv2) that speak CASTV2 protobuf over TLS and drive certified receivers. Building an AirPlay SENDER is harder than a Cast sender because you must produce valid FairPlay/pairing material, but is less explored than the receiver side. For media-URL casting, the 'transmitter' is really an HLS/DASH/CMAF origin/packager, which is fully open (Shaka Packager, ffmpeg, Bento4); DRM only enters if you encrypt segments with CENC and run a license server. Miracast sources exist natively on Windows/Android. Note the asymmetry: a sender can often be told to skip/relax auth in dev builds, but that does not help receiver-builders since production senders enforce the receiver's cert/pairing.

contestedClaims.claim: HDCP and DTCP-IP are link protection, NOT DRM — they protect the wire between devices, whereas DRM (FairPlay/Widevine/PlayReady) encrypts the content itself; DRM merely *requires* HDCP downstream as a chain-of-trust condition.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Constantly conflated in marketing and even some engineering docs. The distinction is real and load-bearing for a receiver-builder, but sources blur it; worth stating precisely.

contestedClaims.claim: AirPlay open receivers (shairport-sync/UxPlay) redistribute Apple-produced FairPlay bytes rather than generating them, and rely on that being tolerated on the same precedent as prior projects.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: The exact legal/technical status of the '~568 FairPlay bytes' and whether current iOS versions still accept the reverse-engineered flow changes over time; the '568' figure and 'v3' details come from reverse-eng sources that may be version-specific.

contestedClaims.claim: CENC 'cbcs' (AES-CBC) is FairPlay's mode while 'cenc' (AES-CTR) is Widevine/PlayReady, and CMAF+cbcs now lets a single encrypted segment set serve all three DRMs.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Broadly correct and multi-source confirmed, but 'all three with one key set' has caveats (PlayReady/Widevine added cbcs support at different times; older clients only do cenc). The clean 'one file, three DRMs' claim is slightly optimistic.

contestedClaims.claim: Google Cast receiver is blocked primarily by the per-device SoC-fused private key + Google-signed cert chain, and third-party receivers (AirServer/Reflector) obtained certs through undisclosed/possibly-licensed means.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: How AirServer/Reflector got valid Cast certs is not publicly documented (licensing vs extraction). Also unclear whether *all* sender configurations strictly enforce device auth or whether some legacy/dev paths relax it.

contestedClaims.claim: Modern Chromecast/Cast uses mDNS (_googlecast._tcp, control on TCP 8009) and DIAL is legacy/app-launch; first-gen used SSDP.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Generational specifics (which gen dropped SSDP/DIAL, exact port/service usage) vary across sources and firmware; the high-level split (mDNS now, DIAL for app-launch, SSDP historically) is solid but exact per-generation details are fuzzy.

contestedClaims.claim: AirPlay auth is selected by feature bits with FairPlay (/fp-setup) and MFi (/auth-setup) mutually exclusive, and there is a documented sender-side 'logic bug' where SupportsUnifiedPairSetupAndMFi alone starts no auth.
contestedClaims.whyUncertain: Sourced from a single reverse-engineering site (Emanuele Cozzi); the 'logic bug' observation is an individual researcher's interpretation of behavior, not confirmed by Apple, and may vary by iOS version.

confidence: High on the open substrate layers (discovery, RTSP/RTP, HLS/DASH/CMAF, codecs) and on the shape of the blockers (Cast device certs, AirPlay FairPlay dependency, HDCP/DTCP-IP/DRM licensing). Medium on version-specific and legally-grey details flagged in contestedClaims (exact FairPlay byte handling on current iOS, per-generation Cast discovery specifics, how third parties obtained Cast certs, and single-sourced AirPlay auth-flow quirks).
